stories.body:
Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand

Business live – latest updates

Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.

China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.

China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.

Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.

Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.

“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.

“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.

However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.

Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.

“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.

stories.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
stories.summary: All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket.

About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest.

The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota . The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin .

The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before.

Once around the Earth

The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered something unusual while combining his cornfield for the fall harvest. A circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks in Scott Township, a community in west-central Minnesota.

The Stevens County Sheriff’s Office said it received a phone call reporting the discovery Wednesday.

“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” the Sheriff’s Office wrote on Facebook. “The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field.”

Law enforcement officials said the debris posed no danger to the public. That might not have been true had the object reentered over a more populated area. Space junk routinely falls out of orbit, and fragments of old rockets or satellites sometimes survive the heat of reentry to reach the ground. No one has ever been seriously injured by falling space junk, but there are a few examples of property damage .

Under international law, the country that launched an object into space is liable for any damage it causes on the ground.

What makes the debris in Minnesota unusual is its size —it’s larger than most objects that survive reentry —and the fact that it likely originated from a rocket that fell from space the same day it launched. The upper stage of the Zhuque-2E rocket has a diameter of 11 feet, or 3.35 meters, perfectly matching the size of the object found in Minnesota.

The Zhuque-2E rocket that launched from China on September 15 deployed 10 satellites for the Qianfan, or Thousand Sails, communications network, a Chinese counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. China has launched 258 Qianfan satellites over a series of missions since 2024, on the way to completing an initial constellation of 1,296 satellites, with longer-term ambitions of more than 15,000.

The methane-fueled rocket released the 10 Qianfan satellites into a circular polar orbit at an altitude of roughly 560 miles (900 kilometers) around a half-hour after liftoff. The rocket flew south from China, over Antarctica, then north over the Americas. After deploying its payloads, Zhuque’s upper stage performed a burn to slow its velocity and drop out of orbit.

Normally, deorbiting a spent rocket stage after the end of its mission is a good thing, a responsible practice aimed at limiting the creation of new space debris. Chinese rockets have been a problem in this area before, with unguided reentries and in-orbit breakups in low-Earth orbit. US rockets on low-Earth orbit missions usually reserve enough propellant for guided disposal.

The upper stage from the Zhuque-2E rocket’s previous flight in June broke apart after completing its mission, leaving dozens of pieces of debris in a heavily trafficked part of low-Earth orbit that’s home to the International Space Station and a significant portion of SpaceX’s Starlink broadband network. The good news is the rocket’s altitude was low enough to ensure most of the debris would reenter the atmosphere within a few months.

LandSpace, the company that owns the Zhuque rocket family, has not publicly acknowledged the debris fall over Minnesota. The usual practice for rocket disposals is to steer them toward reentry over the ocean, suggesting the incident on September 15 was perhaps the result of a botched deorbit burn.

stories.title: China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports
stories.summary: Exports have helped offset weak spending at home, but trade tensions and AI doubts cloud its outlook.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026, 03:03 BST

China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports.

The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data.

The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges.

While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook.

China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".

With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year.

Sales of high-tech goods rose by 14.3% while the production of both batteries and industrial robots grew by more than 29%, official figures showed.

Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending.

But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed.

China's economy has struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers.

There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said.

Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added.

'Investing in people': Can China's new push to boost spending revive the economy? Published 10 March

Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses Published 2 days ago

The effects of Beijing's targeted support measures for businesses have yet to be seen, said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics.

Several risks stand out from the data, including China's reliance on a "single external engine" in exports, he added.

The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters.

Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption.

Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home.

In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy.

But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits.

stories.body:
In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics

I s there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.

It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.

The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them.

Earlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship was successfully contained , showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so.

Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state department officially requested that the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed.

The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway with Russia . But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.

stories.title: Reform MSP quits party to sit as independent
stories.summary: Amanda Bland's decision relegates the party to the third-largest group at Holyrood, with one member fewer than Labour.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Amanda Bland represents Central Scotland and Lothians West

Published 19 October 2026, 11:32 BST

MSP Amanda Bland has quit Reform UK Scotland to sit as an independent.

The resignation relegates the party to the third-largest group at Holyrood, with one member fewer than Labour.

A Reform UK source told BBC Scotland News that Bland was "very difficult to work with" and had been called to a meeting on Wednesday to discuss a high turnover of staff in her office.

Bland, who represents Central Scotland and Lothians West, said her "principles and priorities remain unchanged" but gave no details of why she had left the party.

In a statement she said: "I entered politics to champion fairness and common sense, protect women and children, improve public services, support businesses to thrive, and work towards a fairer and more effective criminal justice system.

"As a member of the criminal justice committee, I remain committed to scrutinising legislation, holding the justice system to account and supporting practical measures that improve public safety, protect victims and ensure justice is served.

"Holding the Scottish government to account remains a key priority, and I believe I can best pursue these goals as an Independent MSP."

She said she would not be making any further statements or giving interviews about Reform, and that her focus now was on her responsibilities as an independent MSP.

A Reform spokesperson said: "Amanda Bland should reflect on her reasons for choosing to isolate herself from that team of capable individuals.

"It is incumbent on her to resign as a regional MSP for Central Scotland and Lothians West and allow her constituents to be represented by the next Reform candidate on that list."

Under Holyrood's rules, a list MSP would be replaced by the their party's next candidate at the last election if they resigned.

Bland, a former primary school teacher and police officer, was among 17 Reform candidates to be returned to the Scottish Parliament in May as the party made its electoral breakthrough north of the border.

The party finished in joint second with Labour, behind the SNP on 58 seats.

Former Conservative minister Malcolm Offord leads Reform in Scotland

Reform's cohort, led by former Conservative minister Malcolm Offord, have repeatedly invoked the condemnation of the chamber - most notably after staging a walkout during an independence debate, and by tabling a motion proposing a burka ban .

Currently, Offord is first to question John Swinney at First Minister's Questions every other week, alternating with Labour. The party is now likely to lose that privilege.

Reform UK says its goal is to disrupt a so-called "cosy consensus" in Scottish politics.

Of the 17 MSPs elected under its banner in May, only one had previous experience at Holyrood.

As party leader, Offord has only had a matter of months to try and turn them into a coherent and cohesive political force.

While Bland's resignation was sudden, some kind of fracture in the group has been widely anticipated.

Reform UK's statement on her departure claims the party has a "united team" at Holyrood - something that will attract much scrutiny and speculation.

Reform 'stunts'

Scottish Labour deputy leader Jackie Baillie said: "No one will be surprised to see chaos at the heart of Reform."

She said the party had been "utterly useless at holding the SNP to account or getting results for the Scottish people", adding: "It's been a series of stunts, gimmicks, photo calls and precious little else."

The Scottish Conservatives said there were growing questions about Reform's ability to provide effective opposition to the SNP at Holyrood.

A spokesperson said: "With Nigel Farage's Reform being weak and ineffective at Holyrood, the Scottish Conservatives will continue standing up to the SNP and fighting for Scotland's taxpayers."

Scottish Liberal Democrat David Green MSP said that Reform had been hit by "scandal after scandal".

He added: "I'm sure more and more of its MSPs will be taking a long hard look at what they've signed up for."

The Scottish Parliament confirmed Bland's resignation and said its website , external had been updated accordingly.

stories.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
stories.summary: Character.AI faces claims its bots encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Character.AI faces claims its bots encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents.

This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.

In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.

The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “ reverse acquihire ,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”

A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.

According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.

As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.

Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.

That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.

In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.

However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.

In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.

A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.

“There’s decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren’t built to guard against.”

Not its first rodeo

This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.

In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”

Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded , determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.

Google declined to comment for this story.

In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.

According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.

The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.

Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggling with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.

In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.

That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.

According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.

A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”

The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.

If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.

The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.

“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

This story originally appeared on wired.com .

stories.title: Troubles legacy bill is not an amnesty for soldiers - NI secretary
stories.summary: Amendments to the bill will be debated by MPs, as the long-awaited legislation returns to the House of Commons.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Troubles was a period of conflict which lasted for 30 years and cost the lives of more than 3,500 people

Published 19 October 2026, 00:00 BST

The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has rejected claims that planned changes to the government's Troubles legacy bill amount to an "amnesty" for former soldiers.

Sir Chris Bryant said it was "completely wrong" to suggest a requirement for the attorney general to consent to serious Troubles-related prosecutions was designed to pardon veterans.

The proposal is among a series of government amendments which MPs will debate on Monday as the long-awaited legislation returns to the House of Commons.

Speaking to BBC News NI, Bryant said it was a "sensible measure" to ensure there was "more consistency" in how decisions are made.

The legislation seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict in Northern Ireland, which cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.

It was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government.

More on this story

NI Secretary defends planned changes to Troubles bill Published 5 days ago

Attorney general approval required for serious Troubles prosecutions Published 6 days ago

New legislation on Troubles legacy deal introduced in Westminster Published 14 October 2025

The government has said its amendments would "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.

While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Sinn Féin has branded the amendments a "veterans' charter".

The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has also raised concerns that MPs will not have enough time to scrutinise the proposed changes.

Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant said the bill will help Troubles victims' families

Sir Chris defended his plans for the attorney general to give consent to serious prosecutions, saying it was a recommendation in a recent Westminster human rights committee.

"We're not carving the Public Prosecution Service in Northern Ireland out of the process," he said.

"They're going to be working with the Crown Prosecution Service in England and Wales to make sure that they've got the same kind of rules and guidelines that apply to all of the prosecutions."

"The attorney general often exercises this kind of role. It's very different from their normal role, but it is something they do quite often."

'Control and cover up' fears

Mark Thompson from the victims' group Relatives For Justice said he feared the bill could lead to unlawful killings being covered up by the state.

"Essentially, this impacts the victims of collusion and state violence," he told the BBC's Sunday Politics programme .

He accused the government of trying to take "control" away from local courts because it did not like some of the recent rulings in Troubles-era cases.

He pointed out that judges had ruled against the Army in "dozens" of inquests into killings carried out by soldiers, including those at Ballymurphy and Springhill .

Thompson argued that local courts had provided a "level playing field" but instead the government caved under pressure from the Army veterans' lobby in London.

"What they [the government] want to do is lift it out of a rule of law process and bring it to London and have a political decision."

Veterans wanted 'Supreme Court judge'

However, lawyer Philip Barden, who has represented several ex-soldiers, claimed Army veterans were "put through the mill" in cases where there was "no evidence".

"What we want is an independent process so its not the PPS and the DPP deciding in Northern Ireland who it is who should be prosecuted," Barden told the programme.

"We wanted a Supreme Court judge as being the most independent person that we could conceive of - not being a political appointment.

"The government have come up with the attorney general of the UK, who of course makes many decisions to prosecute people."

A spokesperson for the PPS said the organisation has "considerable experience in the prosecution of legacy cases".

"We will continue to approach our decision-making with complete impartiality and independence and in accordance with our Code for Prosecutors."

They added: "The proposed role for the Advocate General for Northern Ireland in relation to legacy prosecutions is a matter of government policy and ultimately for Parliament."

Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan Smith (centre left) supported a veterans' protest in London last month

Barden defended the government's choice, saying if people disagreed with the UK attorney general's decisions they could always seek a judicial review, arguing that there was "complete independence".

He added that veterans' "primary cause of concern" was the number of repeat investigations into Troubles cases, despite a lack of any new or compelling evidence.

'Too much politics'

Natasha Butler's grandfather, Paddy Butler, was killed by the Army on the Springhill estate in Belfast in July 1972.

She said she wants to "ensure victims and survivors are not lost in the politics surrounding this bill".

She added that "families have waited decades" for answers and the next generations "inherit the same silence".

David Crabbe served in the Ulster Defence Regiment and the Royal Irish Regiment during the Troubles from 1977 to 2007.

He feels "there has been too much politics at play in this" and called on the bill to be "victim-centred".

He added that "there has been a very narrow focus" on veterans.

'A work in progress'

Joe McVey says the the bill is "not perfect", but is keen to see it progressed

The commissioner for victims and survivors for Northern Ireland said legislation "needs to be truly victims centred".

Speaking on Good Morning Ulster , Joe McVey described the bill as "not perfect", but added "we're very keen that the bill is progressed" as it is "still a work in progress" and needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.

"When you look at the Troubles' Bill, we think there's an absence on a focus on victims and survivors and I think that's the message we keep trying to make very clear."

He added: "If we don't do it this time, then I think it'll be very difficult to predict when it's going to get a hearing again."

Why is Labour bringing this bill?

It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act , which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents.

The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful.

Labour's bill involves a legacy commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.

What is the government proposing to change?

The government said:

The legislation will make clear the commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the armed forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism"

The attorney general, currently Ellie Reeves, will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions

There would be measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the commission's work

Before any witness can be approached, the commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information"

The commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating

Former paramilitaries are barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and there is a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel

There is a statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended"

Opposition parties and backbench MPs have also tabled separate amendments aimed at changing the bill, but it is up to the Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle to decide whether any of them will be accepted for debate.

stories.title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
stories.summary: Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's government.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's government.

Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.

The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.

Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.

What will happen during the vote?

Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.

They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).

Results will then be published as they come in.

At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.

What has led to the vote?

Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.

The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.

Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.

Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.

"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.

Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.

The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.

"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.

Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this .

Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner .

US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months .

When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario .

stories.title: Rubio visits India with a trip to the world's largest oil refinery topping the agenda
stories.summary: A visit to India this week by Washington's top diplomat will skip New Delhi and instead include the world's largest oil refinery, which processes massive amounts of Russian crude. Is Trump looking for a new deal?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A visit to India this week by Washington's top diplomat will skip New Delhi and instead include the world's largest oil refinery, which processes massive amounts of Russian crude. Is Trump looking for a new deal?

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.

Rubio's business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India's purchases of Russian oil .

Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil . The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it's a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India's energy relationship with Russia.

In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.

US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.

An elusive US-India trade deal

Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India's continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In February 2026, Trump announced a "trade deal" that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.

While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India's deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India's top supplier of crude oil.

In mid-September, Trump signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act," imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India .

However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions .

Rubio: Trade deal 'very close'

Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the "C5+1" diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.

"We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said.

"We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio added.

In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.

Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

He said Jamnagar is an "important node in global trade" because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.

Although Trump's sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.

Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio's decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.

"The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar," she told DW. "The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue."

Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.

Shankar pointed to Reliance's proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is "one of the states in play" in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.

"Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome," she said.

Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump eroding trust in Delhi?

The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy.

Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.

"Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values," he said.

The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.

Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.

On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.

The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.

Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump's own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.

"Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians," Pant told DW.

Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump's presidency.

"The sense that America is unreliable, that America can't be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse," he said.

The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.

"If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals "will have consequences."

stories.title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
stories.summary: Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73. A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark Reno v. ACLU ruling in 1997. When the internet was still young, Steinhardt became one of the first attorneys to specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy . In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999. In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based Privacy International . Steinhardt chaired the 2003 Computer Freedom and Privacy Conference and served on a wide variety of significant panels and boards, including the Department of Transportation’s Negotiated Rule Making on national driver’s license standards, the Advisory Committee to the US Census, and the Blue Ribbon Panel on Genetics of the National Conference of State Legislatures. He also was selected to be a member of the US delegation to the G-8 Government and Private Sector Tokyo conference on Cyber Crime and served as an advisor to the Czech Helsinki Committee. “Barry led many critical technology and civil liberties fights and was an important mentor to me and others in the field,” said EFF Executive Director Nicole Ozer. “Barry’s influential work across strategy to defend and advance privacy rights and safeguard people against surveillance has made its mark on the law and policy of our digital world and protected the rights and safety of people across the United States and around the world.”

stories.title: Our Lawsuit Against the Trump Administration’s Social Media Surveillance Moves Forward. Here’s What the Court Said.
stories.summary: No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S. Last fall, we sued on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court denied the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a big deal for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning. Our Lawsuit Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to broadly surveil the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. The government is targeting a broad range of views, including criticism of the Trump administration ; support for Palestine or criticism of Israel ; “rationalizing or making light of” Charlie Kirk’s murder; and anything nebulously “hostile” to American culture, founding principles , “traditional American views,” or “our way of life.” It has paired that surveillance with a public intimidation campaign. High-ranking officials have explicitly threatened to punish noncitizens for their online speech, then followed through with a series of terrifying viewpoint-driven enforcement actions. This has led to a significant chilling effect on speech, not just for noncitizens, but also for their families, coworkers, and friends. stories.title: The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life
stories.summary: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed. As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. stories.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
stories.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. stories.body:
Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys

T here are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment for Donald Trump is poor but small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood.

Confidence is generally stable.

This week, the National Federation of Independent Businesses said that its Small Business Optimism Index fell to just below its long-term average, while uncertainty rose slightly. Labor quality was the top concern for 26% of owners and inflation for 20%. Expansion plans weakened, though 17% still plan to add jobs during the next three months.

However, small-business confidence improved significantly in the third quarter, according to the recently published Justworks/US Chamber Small Business Index . Some 72% of the 750 small businesses surveyed say they are comfortable with their current cash flow, but only 27% believe the US economy is in good health. Inflation remains the biggest problem, cited by 54% of owners.

Hiring is not strong, but not weak either.

HR platform Gusto estimated that small businesses added 28,000 jobs in September, making it the eighth consecutive month of employment gains following a decline in January. According to the company’s data, hiring accelerated from August’s revised gain of 18,500 jobs and growth was broad across industries, regions and company sizes, with healthcare and social assistance among the strongest sectors. Particularly notable is that some of the smallest employers continue to participate in the expansion, rather than job growth being concentrated solely among larger companies.

In its latest Small Business Employment Watch report, Paychex, another large HR and payroll processing service (and a client of my company), said that hiring in September essentially matched its 2026 year-to-date average with overall employment among companies with fewer than 50 employees appearing “stable”.

ADP , the country’s largest HR and payroll processing service, reported that US private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, with hiring accelerating for the first time since May following three months of slowing growth. Education and healthcare and leisure and hospitality led the gains, while financial activities and professional and business services were weaker. Importantly for small businesses, establishments employing one to 19 workers added 18,000 jobs. According to ADP, private-sector employers have not shifted into recession mode and although hiring has cooled from earlier periods, businesses are still adding employees.

Intuit painted a slightly different jobs picture. Its Intuit QuickBooks Small Business Index , which is based on data it gathers from its millions of QuickBooks customers, found that employment at US businesses with one to nine employees fell by 7,000 jobs in September and that jobs declined across most sectors and regions.

Revenues remain solid.

Intuit’s QuickBooks data shows that revenues moved sharply up this past month as inflation-adjusted average monthly revenue increased 1.68% and growth occurring in 11 of 12 industries, every region and 19 of 20 states.

Fiserv , a payment-processing service, said that its September data showed improving sales among US small businesses. However, the company reports that consumer behavior remains selective and that traffic has been weaker even as customers spend more when they do shop.

after newsletter promotion

Economic growth continued in the third quarter.

Overall, US manufacturing remained firmly in expansion territory in September. The Institute for Supply Management’s Manufacturing Purchasing Manager’s Index marked its ninth consecutive month of growth after years of contraction. Despite rising prices, new orders, production and employment all remained expansionary and order backlogs increased. As usual, the ISM reported yet another month of expansion in the service sector (it’s been 27 consecutive months) with new orders remaining “particularly strong”.

The Wall Street Journal and other media sources reported recently that first-quarter annualized growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%, and second-quarter growth was increased to 2.2% from 1.5%, which, its editors argued , shows that the “US economy is performing considerably better than pessimistic headlines imply”.

Philadelphia lags in business creation.

My business is based in Philadelphia, a heavily Democratic area in a swing state. My clients appear to mostly be doing well so far this year but, like most small businesses around the country, continue to struggle navigating higher costs and a tight labor market.

This anecdotal evidence is somewhat supported by a May survey by WSFS Bank that found “surprisingly strong confidence among Philadelphia-area businesses” despite inflation and economic uncertainty. In that study, 92% of owners and business decision-makers say their companies are meeting or exceeding expectations, while 66% anticipate growth during the next year.

Philadelphia, however, has its own unique problems, particularly adding fewer small businesses per capita than other large cities. A recent study from Pew Research found that the number of Black-, Hispanic- and female-owned small businesses increased 39% between 2012 and 2022, showing meaningful entrepreneurial growth, but barriers including access to capital, regulatory requirements, taxes, commercial space and the difficulty of scaling companies continued to restrain business formation in the city.

The Democratic strategist James Carville once said that when it comes to electing candidates, “it’s the economy, stupid”. The good news for the Republicans is that the economy is resilient and the overall mood of the country’s small businesses is generally optimistic, despite the many challenges they face. But will that overcome the president’s low approval ratings?

stories.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
stories.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026, 00:28 BST

The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".

He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.

The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.

It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.

Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.

"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.

"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.

"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."

The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.

The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".

"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine

Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.

But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.

All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".

At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.

Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.

Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.

"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."

"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."

Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".

"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

Long before Silicon Valley promised frictionless, universal solutions to how we live, people in the UK were re-imagining domestic life and the conditions of living from the ground up.

These forms of radical living, whether individual choices or wider movements, were born of dissent , necessity and the desire to live in ways society otherwise sought to restrict. This includes expressions of sexuality, religion, politics and identity. Some began as attempts to create households that escaped prevailing conditions of oppression. Others pursued utopian ideals or organised political campaigns enacted through the very conditions of everyday life.

What the state treated as radical was often, for those living it, the basics of a stable life and an attempt to escape oppression. Though their alternatives were often precarious and sometimes short lived.

Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK , a new exhibition at the William Morris Gallery in Walthamstow, explores how people, places and ideas connect. The show aligns with author Ursula Le Guin’s critique of history by questioning whose stories get told and who tells them.

In her 1986 essay The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction , Le Guin argues that early human history is usually told as a hunting story, centred on a man with a spear bringing down a mammoth. “That story not only has action, it has a hero,” she explains. For this hero, “the proper shape of the narrative is that of the arrow or spear, starting here and going straight there”. Meanwhile, the people gathering food are sidelined.

Le Guin argued that the first human tool was probably a container used for gathering, rather than a weapon. Building on this idea, she suggests that stories can also function like carrier bags, gathering multiple people and ideas together rather than focusing on a single hero.

Earthly Paradise at the William Morris Gallery follows this thinking. The show explores how the home, which Le Guin calls “another, larger kind of pouch or bag, a container for people”, has served as a space to challenge societal norms since the late 18th century. Indeed, Le Guin explicitly lists “the museum” as one of her essential containers, alongside “the medicine bundle” and “the shrine”.

A container for people

The lower gallery focuses on domestic objects and unconventional ways of living. Exhibition labels and press materials highlight how money and class enabled these lifestyle experiments.

Many radical domestic projects relied on substantial wealth, including Morris’s own, which was funded by his father’s investments in the Devon Great Consols copper mine – a venture built on far from utopian working conditions.

A 1947 photograph shows artist Madge Gill surrounded by fabric in her East Ham house. Nearby, photos of Prospect Cottage , Derek Jarman’s Dungeness home following his HIV diagnosis, sit alongside images of 575 Wandsworth Road in south London, created by Kenyan-born poet Khadambi Asalache . After buying the house in 1981, Asalache spent 19 years covering its walls with hand-cut fretwork from reclaimed pine. Together, these images show the home as a refuge, nurture and creative space.

Read more: Why the Dungeness landscape is so inspirational for writers and artists

Upstairs, the focus shifts to radical housing born of precarity and necessity. Fusions Jameen was a Black-led self-build cooperative in Lewisham. Members contributed over 1,000 hours of manual labour for discounted tenancies. It’s an arrangement the group’s chair Tim Oshodi termed “sweat equity”. Oshodi notes in the exhibition catalogue: “You shouldn’t build out of greed; you’re building out of need.”

The show traces connections from Danièle Lamarche’s 1980s photographs of Bangladeshi squatters in east London to a new commission by British artist Delaine Le Bas. Drawing on her Romani heritage, Le Bas combines painting, performance photography and activist documents into a large collage.

One featured photograph shows a toy caravan above a handwritten note: “If I was Sindy would you love me more?” Here, the Sindy doll represents conventional domestic ideals, questioning whether conformity would gain Romani people their denied rights. While children view toy caravans as symbols of freedom, the rightwing press often frames them with prejudice.

Sunil Gupta’s mid-1990s digital photo-montage Trespass 2 is set in the London home he shared with his partners. Bringing his work indoors into the kitchen, Gupta traces how a kitchen makeover by a third party contributed to his relationship’s demise. He layers images of daily domestic life with gay iconography and south Asian cultural artefacts, such as a Madhur Jaffrey cookbook cover. The work highlights, in Gupta’s words, “how a domestic space might also be a contested cultural site”.

By bringing these disparate struggles together, Earthly Paradise highlights the diverse experiences shaping contemporary life. It demonstrates how modern living frequently echoes historical ways of life, albeit under evolving social and political conditions.

Somewhere in particular

The radical experiments of the lower gallery, several of which foregrounded socialism, now find an echo in the utopian rhetoric of Silicon Valley.

Tech billionaires often present their tools as engines of collective abundance. This is typified by OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman’s promises of “shared prosperity to a degree that seems unimaginable today” . What this tech-utopian vision routinely leaves out, however, is the question of for whom this wealth is actually produced, and at whose expense.

That promise of emancipation through technology is made to everyone and to nowhere in particular. By contrast, every collective action depicted in Earthly Paradise is rooted in a particular place.

In the exhibition’s press release , curator Hadrian Garrard states that the show examines how the home acts as a site for challenging societal norms and explores “what the possibilities are for this in today’s world”.

That ambition could readily extend to a digital exhibition space. Rather than reinforcing online hate and conspiracy, a digital gallery could demonstrate how networked platforms foster collective organisation and grassroots change. Without the possibilities such counter-spaces afford, our homes will increasingly be shaped by Silicon Valley’s radical ideologies – leaving us with ways of living we never actually chose.

stories.body:
Late last year, scientists in Germany published some remarkable findings on a second world war munitions dump in the Baltic Sea. Some may dismiss the dump as hazardous waste , but to marine biologists it was something far more exciting: a thriving ecosystem .

Over the decades, the dump has become home to mussels, crustaceans, fish and marine plant life, creating a full community under the sea. It’s a perfect example of an accidental reef, highlighting nature’s ability to reclaim even dangerous human detritus.

Around the UK coast, there are thousands of famous wrecks . I have had the pleasure of diving on many of them, witnessing first hand how sea creatures turn rusting hulls into habitat. Further afield, deliberate artificial reef projects, from Australia to the Caribbean, are evidence that where structures sink, life follows.

But let’s not romanticise our wrecks. While these structures offer a foothold for life, they can also leak toxic compounds into the oceans.

Scuppered ships

Not all reefs are born from disaster. Around the world, governments, scientists and conservation groups have deliberately sunk ships, concrete structures and even old underground train carriages to create new marine habitats. These artificial reefs are designed to mimic the ecological functions of natural reefs , boosting biodiversity and providing refuges for overfished species. They also draw scuba divers and recreational fishers, providing economic incentives for people who live nearby.

In the US, the decommissioned aircraft carrier the USS Oriskany was famously sunk to create a tourist attraction off the Florida coast: the “Great Carrier Reef”. In November 2026, an even bigger ship will be sunk nearby: the SS United States, an ocean liner larger than the Titanic.

In Japan, concrete blocks have been used extensively to stabilise coastlines and provide habitat for fish. In Australia, the “rigs-to-reefs” initiative means old oil rigs – too costly to remove – are being left in place to create new ecosystems .

But there’s a fine line between “marine habitat creation” and simply “dumping unwanted stuff”. Poorly planned projects have often done more harm than good.

Perhaps the most infamous case is the Osborne Reef off Florida. In the 1970s, millions of used vehicle tyres were sunk to create a massive reef. But the steel clips holding them soon corroded, and many tyres broke loose and started scouring the seafloor and battering a nearby natural coral reef during storms.

The expensive lesson is that artificial reefs can at best supplement conservation, but they are not a substitute for protecting natural habitats.

A less visible legacy

Shipwrecks and artificial reefs also bring with them a less visible legacy of metal pollution.

The vast majority of wrecks are made of steel, iron, copper and various other alloys that slowly corrode in seawater. This releases dissolved metals into the surrounding environment, and while iron and steel often rust away harmlessly, other metals can be more problematic.

Copper, zinc, lead, tin and aluminium can leach from hull coatings, machinery, or electrical components. These trace metals and toxic chemicals don’t just wash away. Instead, they accumulate in surrounding sediments and, more worryingly, in the tissues of marine organisms. This is particularly concerning for filter feeders such as mussels and oysters, which can concentrate pollutants and pass them up the food chain to predators – and potentially humans.

In high enough concentrations, these substances become toxic, affecting growth, reproduction and survival. For instance, for many years ship’s hulls were coated with the chemical tributyltin (TBT) to prevent barnacle growth which slows vessels down. However, TBT also caused serious environmental damage: some female dogwhelks developed male sexual organs , for instance, disrupting reproduction cycles in these key coastal molluscs.

The issue is magnified for wrecks that still contain fuel or munitions. Corroding shells and tanks not only release components of explosives but also heavy metals such as mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium, chromium and TNT degradation products.

The Baltic Sea munitions, for example, are slowly leaking toxicants into an already fragile semi-enclosed sea. If fish are still there, how bad can the contamination really be? The problem is that presence does not equal a safe zone. Many toxic metals and explosive residues cause sub-lethal effects that do not immediately drive fish away or kill them outright. Instead, these substances accumulate through the food web. Fish may continue to hang out in contaminated areas while suffering impaired reproduction, altered behaviour, suppressed immune systems, or developmental defects. These effects are ultimately largely invisible without detailed study.

In a semi-enclosed system like the Baltic Sea, limited water exchange exacerbates the problem: contaminants persist longer, sediments act as long-term reservoirs, and chronic exposure becomes unavoidable. What looks like ecological resilience can therefore mask a delayed population collapse, and increased risk to predators, including humans, who potentially consume the fish.

We know that organisms can tolerate pollution in the short term. The question is whether ecosystems can remain functional and safe under decades of continuous, low-level toxic exposure.

Supplement not substitute

The urgent need to create artificial habitats is heightened by the crisis facing natural coral reefs from climate change, ocean acidification, overfishing and pollution. Rising sea temperatures are already triggering mass coral bleaching events.

In this context, wrecks and artificial reefs also serve as accidental laboratories. They show how quickly life will colonise and exploit a new habitat, providing lessons for restoration work elsewhere. But the answer to the reef crisis isn’t simply “sink more ships”.

Artificial reefs should never be seen as a licence to pollute or a shortcut for true conservation. They must complement, not replace, efforts to protect and restore natural habitats. We can’t “offset” destroying an ancient coral reef by sinking an old ship. Conservationists rightly stress the focus must remain on marine protected areas, reducing ocean acidification, tackling overfishing and pollution.

The Baltic Sea munitions “reef” is an accident of history rather than a model for the future. Yes, marine life has flourished there, but it swims in a sea filled with heavy metals and toxins.
