Private Schools, Public Money

Private Schools, Public Money

A high-ranking Republican had wanted only to curb the unchecked growth of West Virginia’s voucher program, not destroy it. In the ensuing backlash, three PACs — affiliated with the Koch family and Jeffrey Yass — helped defeat him at election time.

Co-published with Mountain State Spotlight

On a cold February morning at West Virginia’s Capitol, children in winter jackets, holding signs and their homework, clogged the hallways outside the House Finance Committee room. Delegate Vernon Criss, the committee’s chairperson, popped outside his office, then promptly walked back in.

Five days earlier, the Republican lawmaker had proposed to limit payouts from a voucher program that diverts public tax dollars to private education. Since then, families had shown up each morning, and with them lobbyists and organizers posting inflammatory assertions that the proposal would kill the program.

Criss didn’t want that. Five years earlier, he voted to create the Hope Scholarship program, the nation’s first educational savings account program to have no income requirements. Since then, 11 other states have passed similar legislation.

In the first year of the Hope program in West Virginia, it cost the state $9 million. Now, as 2026 was beginning, it was set to expand, with estimates that it could cost $200 million or more a year. And Criss was concerned that unchecked growth of the program, coupled with a spree of tax cuts, could put the state budget into a tailspin. The state and its lawmakers needed “to face the music,” as Criss would later say.

On that February day in Charleston, a staffer unlocked the committee door. Parents and media filed in, taking seats along the narrow benches lining the committee room’s walls. Kids lay on the floor. A delegate asked if the Hope Scholarship bill would be discussed. When Criss said no, the parents and their kids stood up and filed out.

Within the next few days, lawmakers would stop the effort to curtail spending on vouchers. And Criss would soon be fighting for his political life.

The money and organizing behind the demise of the bill, as well as the targeting of Criss, can be traced to “school choice” advocates at the local and national levels and their ability to spend huge sums to have their way.

When Republicans assumed control of the West Virginia Legislature in 2015, school choice — their preferred terminology for voucher-style programs — became a rallying point for an array of political nonprofits. Through lobbying and supporting sympathetic lawmakers, they helped establish the Hope Scholarship six years later.

The first year, a little more than 2,300 students enrolled in the program , which was designed to permit more students over time. Today, 26,000 students are taking part , more than the enrollment in the state’s largest public school district.

West Virginia has been part of a nationwide push, partially funded by billionaire-backed political groups , to use taxpayer dollars to fund private schools.

Among the proponents of these programs are the influential Koch family network and Pennsylvania billionaire Jeffrey Yass, who has spent more than $350 million since 2015 on political campaigns, including a push for public funding for private education.

In West Virginia, Arkansas and Texas , proponents have been eager to challenge anyone who got in the way, including fellow Republicans who voiced concerns. Basic guardrails or efforts to cap spending have been met with intense resistance.

During the 2026 West Virginia primary, three political action committees spent heavily on independent advertisements, targeting 10 incumbent Republicans. They succeeded in ousting four, all of whom had disagreements with the governor; most expressed reservations about the Hope Scholarship.

Their biggest victory was unseating Criss, the long-serving incumbent and high-ranking Republican.

One of the three PACs working to defeat Criss is affiliated with the Koch family. Yass has contributed to the two others: School Freedom Fund and the Sugar Maple PAC. David McIntosh, president of School Freedom Fund and the affiliated Club for Growth, was jubilant afterward.

“These elections are a warning to Republican leaders like Vernon Criss — if you oppose school freedom, expect to be held accountable,” he wrote in a press announcement at the time.

Help ProPublica Report on Education

Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options.

Criss had been unopposed in his 2024 primary. In 2026, the three PACs spent more than $145,000 to help a 23-year-old defeat him.

Criss’ proposal to put financial limits on the Hope Scholarship program came as West Virginia public schools arrived at a dangerous crossroads. The program directs dollars away from public schools, adding to funding shortfalls created by enrollment drops.

Since 2019, 70 public schools have closed throughout the state, with the system losing more than 30,000 students. By the end of this school year, up to 20 more schools could close.

During the same legislative session this year, when lawmakers passed emergency legislation to help one school district stay open, there was little drama — no crowds in the hallways or the galleries.

The Rise of Hope

In 2021, as West Virginia lawmakers worked on the bill that would create the Hope Scholarship, they got some help from the outside: a lobbyist and political operative named Jason Huffman.

Huffman has been the director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia since the mid-2010s. The group is part of the larger Americans for Prosperity, which was set up by the billionaire industrialist David Koch and supported by his brother Charles, longtime donors to conservative causes. Americans for Prosperity advocates for low taxes, school choice and loosened environmental regulations throughout the country.

In shaping the West Virginia legislation, Huffman said, one goal was to create a school voucher program that other states could model. While other states had already passed voucher-style programs, they hadn’t made them open to all residents regardless of income.

Among those advocating in West Virginia were members of Cardinal Institute, a homegrown conservative think tank. Founded in 2015, the group made public funding for private schooling one of its first policy planks. Over the last decade, Cardinal has received significant donations from organizations that also have received funding from Koch entities and Yass.

To support the Hope legislation, Cardinal’s leaders distributed research, published columns in newspapers and linked up with other groups, like Americans for Prosperity and the Institute for Justice, which litigates libertarian causes, to push the issue. They also found allies in parents who wanted the financial flexibility to send their children to private schools or teach them at home or in small clusters of like-minded families.

Katie Switzer, a mother of six, became one of Cardinal’s most reliable advocates. She had started looking into schooling options after her second child was diagnosed with a learning disability.

“I just felt like this doesn’t feel good to send my nonverbal child to a school that you know isn’t really collaborative, and I don’t know what’s going on when she’s there because she can’t tell me when she gets home,” she said. The experience made her a proponent of alternatives to public school.

Her story appeared in some of Cardinal’s promotional copy for the bill . She sat in on a video call presentation featuring state Sen. Patrcia Rucker, a Hope Scholarship proponent. She took to Facebook to tout the program.

And she stepped up when the Hope Scholarship was challenged in court by other parents who argued the program would undermine funding for public schools.

Hope’s opponents in the case gained support from the state Board of Education, which argued the program siphoned money away from public schools. On the other side was the West Virginia attorney general, Patrick Morrisey, defending the law and the state.

The Institute for Justice was looking to get involved, but it needed to find somebody with standing in the case. Switzer and another parent signed up, giving the firm the ability to file motions and argue in court. The Institute for Justice has received $8.5 million from charities controlled by Yass over nearly a decade.

The case went to the West Virginia Supreme Court, where the justices ruled 4-1 in favor of the program.

The ruling meant the Hope program had survived. It was good timing for Morrisey. He was about to make a run for governor. When Morrisey waded into a tough four-way primary battle, the Club for Growth Action, a super PAC Yass has donated heavily to over the years, was ready to help.

“Our goal in all of this is to elect people who will be champions for school freedom, lower taxes, less regulation, so businesses can thrive,” McIntosh, the group’s president, said in an interview.

The Club for Growth Action pumped $10.8 million into that race. Morrisey won the plurality in the Republican primary and went on to trounce his Democratic opponent in the general election.

On a cold morning in January 2025, Morrisey stood bundled up in a black wool coat on the stairs of Capitol, its gold dome towering above him. He took the oath of office and gave his address.

“We will expand the Hope Scholarship, putting more control in the hands of parents to choose the best educational path for their children,” he said.

Runaway Train

Hours before Morrisey gave his State of the State address earlier this year, the House Education Committee called a meeting to hear about a report from the Rand Corporation, a nonpartisan think tank.

Rand called on the state to fix what was becoming abundantly clear: Education in West Virginia wasn’t just in transition; it was in crisis.

Initially the Hope Scholarship was limited to students attending public school or children who would enter kindergarten. Participation grew over time. And as the 2026-27 school year began, the program opened to any student in West Virginia, including those who had spent their entire academic careers in private school or in homeschooling.

That translated into tens of millions of additional state dollars to private schools and homeschooling. Estimates for the 2026-27 school year ranged from $230 million to more than $300 million in the months leading up to the legislative session. The program costs for the year are still being tallied but are currently projected at an unprecedented $150 million.

The Rand report suggested placing an income cap on the Hope Scholarship and increasing funding for public schools.

While the Education Committee would work on public school funding, Criss’ Finance Committee would tackle the ballooning costs of the Hope Scholarship. He was not interested in Rand’s solutions but found his own. By capping the scholarship amount and limiting certain expenses, Criss was hoping he could help prolong the program for families well into the future. But families would soon be rallying against him.

In the time since the Hope Scholarship had withstood the court challenge, Switzer’s reach had only grown. On Facebook , she administered a group that offers practical advice to hundreds of parents, or “Hope Schoolers” as she called them, on questions like what items counted as qualifying expenses and how to properly file for the program.

Before Criss’ plan rolled out, Switzer said she received word from a member of the Finance Committee — though she did not disclose who — that the Hope Scholarship would be discussed.

Writing a lengthy Facebook post, she warned that the move would severely damage the program. “The bill takes away 19,000 children’s access to online education, tutoring, private schools across state borders, and many other beneficial academic programs,” she wrote.

Huffman, the Americans for Prosperity state director, took to radio and social media to decry what he described as an existential threat to the program. Parents with kids in tow echoed those fears.

Criss’ proposal would’ve capped the award amount for the Hope Scholarship at a little more than $5,000 a year. He said his intent was to prolong the program for the long run, not kill it.

Read More

Huffman countered that by capping the award amount, inflation would eventually erode families’ abilities to use the program for private education or homeschooling.

Looking back, Criss said he anticipated some pushback, because the Hope Scholarship is a “giveaway program.” He blamed political forces for riling people up.

At a caucus meeting with the Republican supermajority — which holds 91 of the 100 seats in the lower chamber — Criss said he couldn’t muster the votes. A bill to fix public schools that came out of the Education Committee died entirely.

Election season was right around the corner, and Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia and other groups hadn’t forgotten the Hope Scholarship battle. Criss had failed what Huffman called “a litmus test” in trying to restrict public money for parents looking for an alternative to public school.

Meanwhile, McIntosh, the president for Club for Growth, said he received word from his allies in the Morrisey administration. Morrisey was concerned about lawmakers who had opposed him on budget issues and school choice. The governor was looking to replace those he saw as not aligned.

While the legislative backlash had been about one issue, the campaign against Morrisey’s foes went well beyond education issues.

Ads depicted Criss as a liberal who wanted to open borders for illegal immigration. That was based on a no vote Criss had cast against a piece of legislation that would’ve mandated employers run a citizenship check on every employee .

Fliers mailed by the School Freedom Fund, a PAC affiliated with Club for Growth, depicted candidates as supporters of drag queens. Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia sent volunteers door to door to rally for their candidates, including in Criss’ district.

The newly created Sugar Maple PAC — headed by a former state delegate and Morrisey ally — ran ads accusing opponents of being Republicans in Name Only.

One mailer, depicting Criss driving a garbage truck, accused him of taking “West Virginia’s values to the dump.” On the back, it reiterated his vote against the citizenship check for employees and his vote against West Virginia’s abortion ban.

“Vernon Criss’ liberal trash,” the flier read, with an image of black trash bags.

“I think that the fact that they called me a liberal, it just stuck out,” Criss said. “You know, as the chairman of finance, I know that it’s a targeted job, obviously, that’s part of the deal. Those types of things happen, that’s just part of the politics involved here.”

The School Freedom Fund poured nearly $1 million into statehouse races across West Virginia to both retain Morrissey’s supporters and oust detractors, like Criss. Americans for Prosperity did the same, again targeting Criss, and spending around $700,000 across the state.

A spokesperson for Morrisey said in an email that the governor is a supporter of both public schools and the Hope Scholarship and “is also grateful that organizations that share his worldview of helping West Virginia children having the best educational opportunities in the country weigh in.”

Sugar Maple PAC and Yass did not respond to requests for comment. Yass contributed $450,000 to Sugar Maple in the lead-up to the 2026 primary. Among the three PACs, Sugar Maple spent the most on the Criss race: $86,000 to attack Criss and $15,000 to back his opponent, Charles Hartzog, a 23-year-old gas station cashier.

Criss didn’t just lose the primary; Hartzog beat him with 61% of the vote. Criss is now running a long-shot campaign as a write-in for his district in the general election.

stories.title: Ken Paxton’s Anti-Abortion Influence Already Extended Beyond Texas. He Could Take It Further in the Senate.
stories.summary: The post Ken Paxton’s Anti-Abortion Influence Already Extended Beyond Texas. He Could Take It Further in the Senate. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A digital collage divided by a red angular border shows Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaking at a microphone in front of the U.S. Supreme Court on the left, juxtaposed with anti-abortion protesters holding a megaphone and a "STOP ABORTION NOW" sign on the right.
stories.body:
Life of the Mother

As Texas attorney general, Paxton has advanced anti-abortion policy in his home state and prevailed where others have failed. Allies who’ve witnessed his victories see an opening to keep moving their cause forward if his Senate bid is successful

Early in his tenure as Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton issued a statement commemorating what he believed was a national tragedy.

“It’s impossible to fill the void of more than 50 million missing human beings,” he said in 2016. He was marking the 43rd anniversary of Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court ruling that protected abortion rights — and had long stood in the way of efforts to ban terminations in early pregnancy, when most abortions occur.

Paxton spent the years that followed testing Roe’s limits and ultimately prevailed where others had failed: In 2021, he defended a near-total abortion ban that Texas legislators had designed to evade conventional legal challenges. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed it to take effect while Roe remained in force.

After the justices overturned Roe the following year, Paxton kept pushing, pursuing new ways to extend the reach of Texas’ restrictions. He prevailed against the Biden administration, picked fights with states that protect abortion access and pioneered strategies that his peers later adopted or expanded.

While Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum for his personal scandals and alleged misuse of the office , detractors and allies alike agree that his signal achievement as the state’s top legal official has been advancing restrictions on abortion.

A close look at his record shows a clear pattern in his successes: He relentlessly tests the limits of the law and employs novel legal strategies to advance his goals.

Paxton’s national role as an anti-abortion warrior would change if he wins his U.S. Senate race. As Texas attorney general, he has been able to act largely on his own authority. If he prevails in November, he would become one of 100 senators in a chamber where most legislation needs 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.

But allies who have witnessed his victories see an opening.

“He’ll have the ability to use some of the laws that he’s defended in Texas as influence to draft legislation in the U.S. Senate,” said Mary Elizabeth Castle, director of government relations at Texas Values, a Christian advocacy group that supports a national abortion ban.

Legal experts and advocates on both sides expect he could join colleagues who are pressuring the Food and Drug Administration to revoke its approval of the abortion drug mifepristone.

Anti-abortion activists at the state and federal level are also trying to secure legal rights for fetuses, which could have implications for reproductive care like birth control and in vitro fertilization. Paxton, who has called himself a strong supporter of IVF, recently said he was open to restrictions intended to prevent the loss of fertilized eggs.

His litigation has also raised questions that experts expect the Supreme Court to confront, including whether a federal law, which mandates hospitals provide stabilizing care to patients having an emergency, overrides state abortion bans; whether to treat a fetus as a separate patient that has its own emergency care rights; and how far states can go in pursuing out-of-state doctors who prescribe abortion medication to patients in states where it’s banned.

During the current race, abortion has played a far smaller role than questions about Paxton’s ethics. His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has said that he supports restoring a federal right to abortion and that his Christian faith calls for an end to “extreme” laws that Paxton has defended and that have forced women to flee the state for emergency abortion care.

Lately, Paxton has said little about abortion — an issue on which he has defended restrictions more stringent than many Texans say they want .

But those who have watched Paxton extend the reach of Texas law beyond its borders are paying close attention to his Senate bid.

Dr. Jennifer Villavicencio, an abortion provider, said she has felt compelled to move her family twice to states with strong laws shielding doctors from out-of-state litigation, partly out of concern that Paxton is creating a blueprint for targeting providers like her.

“It’s very disheartening and scary to think that it’s maybe coming to the U.S. Senate,” she said.

Paxton successfully defended a near-total abortion ban before Roe v. Wade was struck down.

When Paxton became Texas attorney general in 2015, there was no ambiguity about where he stood on abortion.

Raised by an anti-abortion activist , he married his sweetheart from a Christian college, who spoke proudly about the fact that she was adopted , saying her birth mother “ chose life .” She campaigned for Paxton, but he had his own bona fides. A law he’d co-sponsored as a state senator banned almost all abortions after 20 weeks.

Similar 20-week bans had taken root across the country as decades of court rulings chipped away at Roe, but no state had managed to enforce a ban as early as six weeks. More than a dozen tried, passing laws that prohibited abortion when cardiac activity could be detected. One after another, they were blocked by judges.

Then, in 2021, a Texas lawyer named Jonathan Mitchell worked with legislators to craft a law that would withstand similar challenges. Instead of having state officials enforce their “heartbeat law,” the new act, referred to as Senate Bill 8, allowed citizens to sue physicians they suspected were providing abortions. The law offered up to $10,000 if they won.

When abortion providers and President Joe Biden’s administration separately challenged the law in federal court, Paxton’s office argued that state officials couldn’t be ordered to stop enforcing it because they had no power to do so in the first place. Only private citizens could.

“Because the executive officials are expressly prohibited from enforcing SB 8,” his office wrote to the Supreme Court, “there is nothing for a federal court to enjoin.”

The Supreme Court agreed that Paxton couldn’t be sued because “the petitioners have not identified any enforcement authority the attorney general possesses in connection with S. B. 8 that a federal court might enjoin him from exercising.”

The law remained in effect, becoming the first enforceable six-week ban under Roe.

Legislators in Idaho and Oklahoma subsequently passed similar laws.

For Dr. Sam Dickman, who worked at a San Antonio Planned Parenthood, the implications were clear: “I was going to need to either entirely change the type of medicine I was providing or leave the state,” he said. He opted for the latter, moving to Montana, where abortion is legal until viability, or roughly 24 weeks.

Days after the Texas ban took effect, Josseli Barnica arrived at a Houston hospital in the midst of a miscarriage . She was 17 weeks pregnant and her fetus’s head was pressed up against her dilated cervix. Because the situation put her at high risk of developing an infection, medical experts said doctors should have offered to speed up delivery or empty her uterus; the fetus was not viable, and losing the pregnancy was inevitable.

But the fetus’s heart was still beating.

Barnica relayed to her husband what she said her medical providers had told her: “They had to wait until there was no heartbeat,” he told ProPublica in Spanish. “It would be a crime to give her an abortion.”

For 40 hours, Barnica waited, her uterus exposed to bacteria.

She died days later of sepsis. Medical experts told ProPublica her doctors did not follow the proper standard of care and that Barnica’s death was preventable.

In a statement, HCA Healthcare, the hospital chain that treated her, said “our responsibility is to be in compliance with applicable state and federal laws and regulations” and said that physicians exercise their independent judgment.

Paxton blocked federal guidance for emergency abortion care, with consequences far beyond Texas.

When the Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to abortion on June 24, 2022, Paxton dismissed his staff at noon to celebrate. He would later designate the date as a paid office holiday, Sanctity of Life Day.

The Texas Legislature had prepared for the occasion, passing a law that went into effect shortly after the overturning of Roe. The ban threatened doctors with up to 99 years in prison if they performed an abortion. But soon came what Paxton framed as a federal attempt to thwart the state law.

The Biden administration issued a memo to doctors in states with abortion bans saying that a federal emergency care law protected their medical judgment, “regardless of the restrictions in the state.”

The federal Health and Human Services secretary at the time said doctors had an obligation to follow the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act, better known as EMTALA. The law requires hospitals that accept federal funding to screen and stabilize every patient who arrives.

For those with complications such as severe preeclampsia, a potentially fatal, pregnancy-related blood pressure disorder, stabilizing a patient might require performing an abortion, even if the state forbids it, the guidance said. “The physician must provide that treatment,” it said, bolding the word “must.”

Paxton sued, accusing the administration of an attempt to use federal law “to transform every emergency room in the country into a walk-in abortion clinic.”

He argued EMTALA was created to make sure hospitals didn’t dump uninsured patients back on the street without treatment, not to override state laws. He took the argument a step further, suggesting that under EMTALA, doctors might need to consider “the life of the unborn child.”

The argument was novel, six legal experts told ProPublica.

“He’s basically suing the federal government to protect Texas’ right to force pregnant women to not get abortions, even when their health is threatened,” said Greer Donley, a law professor at the University of Pittsburgh. “I remember thinking, ‘Wow, that’s radical.’”

Medical groups warned patients would die.

But a federal judge sided with Paxton that August, and the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the decision in January 2024.

The ruling did more than keep the administration from enforcing its EMTALA interpretation in Texas.

It barred the federal government from pursuing cases against members of two anti-abortion medical organizations that had joined Paxton’s suit as plaintiffs, the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Christian Medical & Dental Associations. This effectively exempted them from having to follow the federal guidance, regardless of where they worked.

It also served as immediate litigation fodder for another state fighting to enforce its own abortion ban.

Idaho had not had the same success in court as Texas. After the Biden administration sued, arguing the state’s ban conflicted with EMTALA, Idaho lost in lower and appellate courts, leaving its ban effectively frozen in emergency cases, with doctors instructed to follow the federal guidance.

But Paxton’s 5th Circuit win on Jan. 2, 2024, gave Idaho’s ban a lifeline. The ruling conflicted with the 9th Circuit’s decision in Idaho, creating the kind of disagreement between federal appeals courts that the Supreme Court often steps in to resolve.

The following day, attorneys representing Idaho asked the high court to do just that, saying Paxton’s success showed they were “likely to prevail.” In the meantime, they asked the court to unfreeze the ban.

On Jan. 5, the Supreme Court allowed Idaho to fully enforce its ban while the case proceeded.

Emergency doctors began hesitating over when they could legally provide abortions, Dr. Jim Souza, chief physician at St. Luke’s Health System, said on a press call at the time, according to NPR . “Is she septic enough for me to do this abortion and not risk going to jail and losing my license?”

In the three months that followed, St. Luke’s, the state’s largest hospital system, said it had to airlift six patients out of the state for abortions.

In Texas, ProPublica has documented the consequences for women experiencing pregnancy emergencies.

When Tierra Walker sought care later that year in San Antonio, she developed preeclampsia and ultimately died from it , ProPublica previously reported. None of the 90 physicians involved in her care offered her the option of terminating her pregnancy, even after she asked if doing so might keep her safe.

Her family sued Paxton in September, along with state medical officials and several healthcare providers, alleging that Texas’ abortion restrictions and the care Walker received led to her death. Paxton has not responded to the suit and did not respond to a request seeking comment.

ProPublica has identified at least two other pregnant Texas women who died without what experts said was appropriate emergency care. Paxton has not publicly commented on any of their deaths and did not respond to ProPublica’s questions about them. Our analysis also found worsening outcomes across the state for patients experiencing pregnancy complications .

The reach of Paxton’s legal victory may not end there.

The Supreme Court still hasn’t resolved the conflict between the circuit rulings. It declined to do so in the Idaho case, and after President Donald Trump took office, his administration dropped the suit and rescinded the EMTALA guidance.

But legal experts told ProPublica the Supreme Court has yet to resolve core questions that Paxton’s litigation raised: whether EMTALA preempts state abortion laws and whether a fetus also has a right to emergency treatment that could conflict with the mother’s interests in cases where her health is at risk.

To guard against future rulings, a reproductive rights advocacy group called All* Above All is pushing state-level legislation to safeguard emergency care. “We’re seeing the chaos right now and the confusion,” said its president, Nourbese Flint.

Paxton tested expansive new ways to pursue abortion providers. Other states are following his lead.

On Dec. 7, 2023, a state judge in Austin issued a ruling that Paxton immediately moved to stop.

A 31-year-old mother named Kate Cox wanted permission to get an abortion. She was 20 weeks pregnant and carrying a fetus diagnosed with trisomy 18, a genetic condition that kills the vast majority of babies born with it.

Texas doesn’t allow abortions for fatal fetal anomalies, but Cox’s doctor argued that if she was forced to give birth, it could imperil her ability to get pregnant again. It was also medically risky: Cox had already had two children by cesarean section, and the chances of complications increase with each procedure.

The day a Travis County district court judge granted her request, Paxton took a step legal experts told ProPublica they had not seen another state attorney general take:

He sent letters to three hospitals where Cox’s doctor had admitting privileges, threatening legal action if the doctor performed the abortion a judge said she could have. The court order, he wrote, did not insulate hospitals, doctors or anyone else from civil and criminal liability for violating Texas’ abortion laws.

At the same time, he appealed the case to the Texas Supreme Court, saying that Cox did not face the kind of threat to her life that fell under the law’s exception. If legislators had wanted to write an exception for fatal fetal anomalies, he said, they would have done so.

“The Texas Legislature did not intend for courts to become revolving doors of permission slips to obtain abortions,” he said.

The Texas Supreme Court agreed with Paxton and reversed the lower court’s ruling. By that time, Cox had sought an abortion out of state.

“It was incredibly scary,” Cox told ProPublica. “We saw in my case that Texas will go after doctors.”

Paxton was also the first — and, so far, the only — attorney general to criminally prosecute a provider in his state for violating an abortion ban.

According to court documents, investigators got an anonymous tip alleging that abortions were being performed at a medical clinic that catered to low-income, Spanish-speaking patients, managed by Maria Rojas, a licensed midwife.

Rojas was arrested and charged with practicing medicine without a license and violating the state’s abortion ban. Paxton also moved to temporarily shut down the clinic and others she ran while the case progressed through court. Months after her arrest, Paxton announced he had arrested and indicted eight other clinic staffers for practicing medicine without a license.

Rojas has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Her attorneys have accused Paxton’s office of a shoddy investigation and argued that at least one case prosecutors were treating as an abortion was actually the management of a patient’s miscarriage.

A trial has not yet been scheduled, but an appeals court this summer overturned the order shuttering the clinics, finding the state had not presented sufficient admissible evidence to justify a temporary injunction. Paxton said he is appealing the ruling. The court did not rule on whether Rojas had actually performed illegal abortions.

Paxton has not stopped at the state border in his pursuit of doctors.

In December 2024, he sued Dr. Margaret Carpenter, a New York-based physician, accusing her of violating multiple Texas laws when she treated a patient via telehealth who lived in Plano, a suburb north of Dallas, and prescribed her abortion medication.

Because the patient was based in Texas, he argued, Carpenter was subject to laws there that banned abortion and required a license to practice in the state.

Carpenter didn’t respond to the suit, so Paxton won by default. But Texas was unable to collect on more than $100,000 in civil fines and court fees that resulted; a New York county clerk refused to register the judgment, invoking a “shield law” that protects providers of abortion care that is legal in New York from certain out-of-state investigations, prosecutions and judgments. At least 22 states have passed shield laws since Roe was overturned, and New York’s is among the strongest. Carpenter did not respond to a request seeking comment and has not publicly responded to the case.

A New York judge dismissed Paxton’s case seeking to enforce the judgment, but Paxton didn’t give up, filing two more civil suits this year against practitioners and organizations in Delaware and California that mail abortion medication to Texas.

Three other state attorneys general have now expanded on the strategy. Last month, Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill — who brought criminal charges against Carpenter after Paxton sued her ( and has faced similar obstacles in New York ) — joined the attorneys general of Arkansas and Alabama in filing a sweeping federal civil suit against out-of-state providers of abortion pills. The case names some of the same providers Paxton pursued; they have challenged the suits. The three attorneys general filed a separate action directly with the Supreme Court asking it to strike down shield laws in New York, Massachusetts and California.

Paxton has moved beyond doctors to target other entities that help patients obtain abortions. Mary Ziegler, an abortion historian and professor of law at University of California, Davis, called him “an innovator in terms of broadening the network of people who were seen as culprits or aiders or abettors.”

He sent cease-and-desist letters to organizations that ship abortion medication into Texas; the attorney general of Alabama subsequently used similar tactics. And Paxton sued cities in his state to stop them from disbursing funds to help women travel for abortions — a move the Legislature followed with a law banning such funding.

Following his legal victory against the city of San Antonio early this year, in which it was forced to end the $100,000 program, Paxton made a vow :

“I will always do everything in my power to prevent radicals from manipulating the system to murder innocent babies.”

stories.title: The Attraction of the Far Right in Brazil
stories.summary: Bolsonarismo lives on despite the incarceration of its leader. The post The Attraction of the Far Right in Brazil appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Flavio Bolsonaro (Shutterstock)

If Flávio Bolsonaro wins the presidential run-off in Brazil on October 25, he would extend the region’s run of Trump-aligned right-wing governments. His opponent, incumbent Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva, ran two percentage points behind Bolsonaro in the first round. No candidate finishing second has won since the institution of democratic elections in 1989. Meanwhile, the remaining candidates that captured nearly 8 percent of the vote are largely center-right.

So, Lula’s chances don’t look particularly strong.

A Bolsonaro win would push Latin America’s largest progressive democracy rightward. It would leave only Claudia Sheinbaum hanging on in Mexico City. This is, in effect, the biggest shift to the right in Latin America since the days of Operation Condor.

The Lula Years and Their Limits

Brazil is no longer the country Lula governed in 2003, nor is it the one that returned him to power in 2023 as a democratic bulwark against Flávio Bolsonaro’s father. Lula’s first administrations benefited enormously from the commodity boom of the 2000s, particularly Chinese demand for agricultural and mineral exports.

Those revenues were put into redistribution, to visible effect. Inequality fell substantially, as around 20 million people were lifted from destitution. Access to electricity, public services, education and healthcare expanded, and university participation rose. Lula’s flagship program, the Bolsa Família, established conditional cash transfers as an effective social-policy instrument. Millions of households acquired consumer goods and financial services previously beyond their reach, while real incomes and formal employment increased. It was a veritable social transformation.

But much of that depended on a one-time commodity windfall that evaporated after 2014, pushing Brazil into recession that lasted until late 2016. The crisis years under Dilma Rousseff exposed the limitation of Lula’s model, which did not convert the commodity tailwinds into sufficient productivity growth and sustained dynamism.

That history matters now. In 2026, unemployment was 5.3 percent in the quarter ending July (though informal private-sector employment rose 3.6 percent over the previous quarter) and GDP growth slowed to 0.5 percent . Household consumption fell 0.4 percent amid high interest rates and indebtedness. Brazil has a severe debt problem, both public and private, making fiscal pressures severe. Gross public debt reached 82.5 percent of GDP in July 2026, well above the 60 percent comfort zone. The interest bill alone consumed 8.7 percent of GDP over the preceding 12 months.

To make matters worse, savings are evaporating, and the investment rate remains merely 16.1 percent of GDP , limiting sustained productivity growth. The central bank has begun easing monetary policy from a near 20-year peak. But with the policy rate still around 14 percent , borrowing costs remain high. Lower rates may offer some relief, but they cannot by themselves resolve the fiscal pressures or reverse Brazil’s chronic investment shortfall.

The challenge, then, is to make Brazil’s social transformation economically durable. The larger lower-middle class created under Lula now wants more than redistribution. It is calling for affordable credit, less bureaucracy, better infrastructure, and greater opportunity. Lula’s exemption of monthly incomes up to R$5,000 from income tax, effective January 2026, is his clearest response. But tax relief and social protection cannot substitute for productivity growth.

These contradictions may soon confront Flávio Bolsonaro. He would inherit an economy where preserving Lula’s gains would require fiscal stabilization, higher investment, and stronger productivity. A movement built on opposition to Lula and reactionary cultural issues has yet to offer an economic model capable of meeting these demands.

Security and Democratic Accountability

The homicide rate fell to 20.1 per 100,000 in 2024, its lowest since the mid-1990s , but organized criminal groups remain powerful. Meanwhile, estimated concealed homicides rose 88.6 percent in a single year, from 3,755 in 2023 to 7,083 in 2024. Once these are included, the apparent improvement in lethal violence becomes considerably less reassuring.

Higher incomes cannot compensate for extortion or unsafe neighborhoods. Stronger state capacity against organized crime requires intelligence, policing, prosecution, and financial enforcement capable of dismantling criminal networks rather than relying on indiscriminate violence.

The October 2025 Rio de Janeiro operation, the deadliest police action in Brazilian history, exposed the limits of the latter approach. More than 100 people died , including four police officers, yet none of those killed appeared on the prosecutors’ list of suspects underpinning the operation, and the gang’s leading figures remain at large. The result was a devastating loss of life without convincing evidence that the organization’s grip on the affected communities had been broken.

Washington’s designation of two Brazilian criminal groups as terrorist organizations, after Flávio Bolsonaro lobbied for it at the White House over Lula’s objections, opens the door to U.S. sanctions and, potentially, military action.

The grievances Bolsonarismo exploits are real, but there is a distinction between a legitimate conservative challenge and Jair Bolsonaro’s legacy. His attempt to overturn the 2022 defeat, his role in the January 8, 2023 attacks, and his conviction for undermining the constitutional order have made democratic accountability unavoidable. Sentenced to 27 years and in custody since August 2025, he has nevertheless seen Congress soften that accountability. In April 2026, it overrode Lula’s veto of a sentencing law that could reduce his term to around 22 years; Justice Alexandre de Moraes suspended the law pending a constitutionality ruling. The Supreme Court resisted threats to constitutional government, though its extraordinary measures have raised concerns about judicial overreach.

Meanwhile, Bolsonaro’s family remains central to Brazilian politics. Wife Michelle and sons Carlos and Jair Renan won congressional seats on October 4, while another son, Eduardo, has sought U.S. pressure over his father’s prosecution. Flávio has pledged amnesty, making a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency another potential test for the Court.

Pentecostal churches are central to this coalition because they have expanded precisely among the urban poor who once formed much of the Brazilian left’s social base. They offer community, practical support, and a language of individual advancement in the place of government services. The Bolsonaros’ emphasis on family and opposition to abortion and LGBTQ rights has helped turn this constituency into a powerful source of political support.

As Fernando Brancoli argues in Bolsonarismo : The Global Origins and Future of Brazil’s Far Right , however, the movement behind Flávio is a fragmented coalition of neo-evangelicals, military actors, and market-oriented ideologues, increasingly connected to international far-right networks. Antipetismo (opposition to Lula’s Workers’ Party, the PT) and evangelical churches anchor it more firmly than Milei-style liberalism.

Brazil in the World

Lula has long treated foreign policy as development politics, using Brazil’s Global South weight to promote multilateralism, South-South cooperation, and autonomy. In Africa, this includes renewed engagement with the Portuguese-speaking world: Brazil joined the African Development Bank’s Lusophone Compact in 2024, while the state oil company Petrobras resumed African exploration. The Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries gives Brazil an institutional presence in Africa unmatched elsewhere in Latin America.

Globally, Lula’s government hosted the 2025 BRICS summit, used Brazil’s G20 presidency to launch a global alliance against hunger, and hosted COP30 in Belém, where Brazil launched the Tropical Forest Forever Facility with more than $6 billion in initial pledges.

Under Jair Bolsonaro, by contrast, Amazon deforestation surged by about 60 percent , with more than 45,000 square kilometers cleared between 2019 and 2022, making fears of renewed extractive pressure under Flávio more than hypothetical.

BRICS is also where the camps differ most visibly. Flávio has said he would reassess membership, while Lula’s diplomacy has sought a global progressivism that is neither subordinate to Washington nor defined by anti-Westernism, though his positions on Ukraine and Taiwan among others betray the influence of Moscow and Beijing. Nonetheless, even Lula has opposed the bloc’s expansion and sought to keep BRICS reformist rather than revolutionary.

Neither candidate has a clear strategy for managing dependence on China, which sets a hard limit on Brazilian autonomy, regardless of the party in office. Beijing bought about $100 billion of Brazilian goods in 2025, comprising nearly 29 percent of Brazil’s exports, including most of its exportable soybeans, iron ore, and oil. With the Brazilian right dependent on the agribusiness lobby, even Jair Bolsonaro’s anti-China rhetoric faded in office. He stayed in BRICS and even hosted its 2019 summit.

Flávio’s program proposes joining the U.S.-led Shield of the Americas, seeking a bilateral free-trade agreement, offering Washington concessions on rare earths, energy, and agribusiness, and keeping its PIX instant payment system away from non-Western settlement arrangements. But absent pragmatic negotiation with Beijing, he too may have little room for maneuver.

Trump’s Shadow

Since 2025, Washington has used visa restrictions, Magnitsky sanctions, tariffs, and terrorist designations against Brazilian targets, including measures tied to the Bolsonaro case. Eduardo Bolsonaro claimed credit after a 50 percent tariff was announced against his own country, though it was later struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court. In July 2026, Washington imposed new Section 301 duties of 25 percent, plus a further 12.5 percent on Brazilian goods, citing PIX, Brazilian court orders against U.S. social-media platforms, ethanol, and deforestation. U.S. officials have portrayed Justice Moraes’s orders against hate speech as censorship, turning Brazil’s regulation of digital platforms into a trade dispute.

The broader context is Trump’s renewed assertion of U.S. influence in the Western hemisphere, reviving the controversial Monroe Doctrine. The Trump administration sees Brazil as a major remaining obstacle to a sweep of Trump-aligned governments in its “backyard” after the removal of Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela, intense pressure on Cuba, and right-wing victories in Chile, Colombia, Honduras, and Peru.

Brazil’s defining question is what follows should the far right win again. Flávio Bolsonaro’s political inheritance and growing alignment with the Trump administration would confront a country whose social transformation has created demands it cannot easily satisfy. Whether Brazil’s institutions can contain that coalition, while preserving the gains and democratic freedoms of the past two decades, may determine not only the country’s future but the direction of Latin America as a whole.

stories.title: Washington’s Diesel Waiver Ends the Moral Case for Secondary Sanctions
stories.summary: Trump's double standard on Russian energy exports will have a corrosive effect on relations with India and other countries. The post Washington’s Diesel Waiver Ends the Moral Case for Secondary Sanctions appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

In August 2025, Donald Trump put an extra 25 percent tariff on Indian goods because New Delhi kept buying Russian oil, lifting the total duty to 50 percent. India held out for more than five months. In February it gave way. Trump’s executive order lifting the penalty recorded that India had committed to stop importing Russian oil “directly or indirectly.”

On October 9, Washington became a buyer itself. After a phone call with Vladimir Putin, Trump announced that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 tons in November, a million tons after that and then another 3 million. Within hours, the Treasury issued General License 135 , authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel, including into the United States, until April 7, 2027. The 2022 law banning Russian energy imports is still on the books.

Buying fuel during a shortage is not the scandal. The asymmetry is. India was told that Russian barrels paid for a war and that buying them carried a price. Washington has now decided that the same barrels become acceptable once American pump prices collide with an election calendar, and it made that trade for what amounts to about a week’s worth of diesel by one estimate. A sanctions regime that bends to the enforcer’s fuel bill stops working as a principle. It works as a price instrument, and every energy importer in the Global South will now treat it as one.

The sequence explains the decision. Ukrainian drones spent the summer hitting Russian refineries, and Moscow banned diesel exports on July 8. In late September, Trump asked Zelensky to scale back the strikes; a U.S. official told Axios that Kyiv ignored six such requests. U.S. diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on September 22 and still averaged $6.23 on the day of the call, with midterms set for November 3. A G7 pledge to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel had not moved the pump price, and neither had an executive order freeing truckers to burn tax-exempt dyed diesel. Russian supply was the lever left.

Moscow priced that lever in public. On September 25, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Russian diesel could saturate world markets but only sanctions stood in the way, which Putin confirmed at the Valdai forum on October 1. Eight days later Washington removed the obstacle that Putin and Peskov had named. What it received in return on the war was nothing: during the 90-minute call, Putin declined to commit to resuming peace talks with Ukraine.

The fine print matters more than the headline tonnage. Trump tied the largest tranche, 3 million tons, to “the condition of their Diesel Refineries.” That clause gives Washington a commercial stake in the very plants Ukraine has spent months trying to shut down. Zelensky called the arrangement “not fair and not honest,” noting that it was announced while his negotiators sat with U.S. envoys in Miami. The next day, Trump blamed Zelensky for American diesel prices and said Ukraine needed a new president. Russian glide bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia that same Saturday.

Then there is the law Trump signed in September. It directs the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas. Washington is now obliged to threaten its trading partners with triple-digit tariffs for buying Russian energy while it buys Russian energy. Republicans have noticed. Senator Thom Tillis said the deal may be illegal. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick is pushing a bipartisan bill to block it. Nebraska’s Don Bacon , whose state runs on farm and freight diesel, wrote that lower prices are needed “but buying Russian fuel is the wrong answer.” Treasury says it will proceed under existing authority.

Europe keeps exemptions of its own. On September 22, the EU dropped Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its blacklist under pressure from France and Luxembourg, the price for extending sanctions on some 3,000 others for three years. Western sanctions on Russia have always carried carve-outs. What changed on October 9 is that the largest one went to the government that wrote the rules for everyone else.

From South Asia, none of this is abstract. When the penalty tariff landed, India’s foreign ministry called it unfair, unjustified, and unreasonable, pointing out that other countries were buying the same oil untouched. New Delhi paid anyway. Its exporters absorbed a 50 percent U.S. duty, and relief came only after it promised to give up discounted Russian crude in a year when the Iran war had already squeezed Gulf supply. Nobody in Washington issued India a six-month general license. Pakistan and Bangladesh, which import most of their fuel and hold no leverage in Moscow or Washington, simply paid the higher diesel bill.

The logic now runs in only one direction. If affordable diesel justifies an exemption for farmers in Nebraska, it justifies one for farmers in Punjab, on either side of the border, and for bus operators in Nairobi. Restrictions that move world energy prices should be negotiated where the countries paying for them have a voice, starting at the United Nations. They should not arrive as a Treasury license issued on a Friday afternoon less than four weeks before a midterm vote.

Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said that Russia-U.S. cooperation on diesel “will benefit the world.” On prices, he may be right. The next time Washington asks an Asian refiner to walk away from a discounted Russian cargo, though, the refiner will have a one-word reply ready: diesel.

stories.title: When The Present Eats The Future
stories.summary: The post When The Present Eats The Future appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Achilles heel of consumer democracies.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled “Americans Are Losing The Long Game” is excellent on this point.

While state-guided dirigiste policies that champion and support strategic industries deemed critical for the future are roundly frowned upon in market economies, the opposite rigidity of the short-term consumerist mentality is less appreciated as a critical failure of good governance. Yet, unless societies prepare for, subsidize and invest in the kind of future they want, they will never get there.

“The present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society.”

China’s Market-State Modality

Of all the major powers, post-Mao China stands out in taking control of its future without sacrificing the present. Over recent decades, it has both lifted hundreds of millions into general prosperity while, at the same time, swiftly conquering the key industries of a sustainable future, from green technology to artificial intelligence.

One has to admit that the Middle Kingdom’s mix of a long-term planning framework checked by robust market signals and bolstered by strategically deployed subsidies has worked. Indeed, it has worked too well: Its overproduction is spilling out and flooding world markets, threatening to displace domestic jobs and industry elsewhere.

China has not arrived at this point overnight. It has been a long time coming. In 1987, the ideology chief of the Communist Party politburo at the time, Hu Qili, told me in Beijing: “The market is not a feature unique to capitalism. Capitalism does not have the patent right over the market economy. What we are trying to create is a new and unprecedented modality where planning is combined with the commodity economy, where the state regulates the market, and the market guides the enterprises.”

The overall economy is steered by a one-party political system designed to reach consensus over long-term goals that have the decisive thrust to be carried out over many years without a break in continuity. Once set, the policy path is followed with relative discipline by a leadership and administration that, while not based on popular appeal to an electorate, is systemically accountable for realizing its set objectives.

When a key strategic goal is ordained by the Party, the state fosters a “whole dragon” approach in which start-up subsidies, sourcing, supply chains and production capacity are vertically aligned, making it one of the most powerful production ensembles in economic history.

Flaws Linked To Strength

The chief flaw of China’s system, of course, is closely linked to its strength. To keep the consensus from fraying, it overcompensates on the side of repressive order and control of freedom. It is the opposite of the open societies of the West, where the flaw lies within the strength of diverse participation and electoral competition: a growing inability to forge a consensus on long-term goals out of the cacophony of voices, the welter of contending interests and the immediate wash of fickle public opinion.

When all-out competitive partisanship destroys consensus among the body politic, the democratic transfer of power can mean a complete rupture of policies endorsed by most voters only four years earlier. Sticking to the course for the time it takes to reach fruition is not a reliable feature of this system.

The extreme edge of this stark difference can be seen in the contrasting behavior of the current leadership in the U.S. and China. America’s leader relishes dominating the memes of the moment, battling his way through every 24-hour news cycle by firing off social media barrages at sundry foes. China’s near-dictatorial leader has used his amassed clout to chart out a roadmap for the next half century.

China’s Long March To Owning Green Technologies

Meeting in Mexico in 2012, the G-20 decided for the first time to put climate change on the agenda. In those days, the Berggruen Institute’s 21 st Century Council, a group of former heads of state and government, tech leaders and Nobel laureates, would meet with the chair of the G-20 each year to advise on its agenda. Read Noema in print.

That year’s chair, then Mexican president Felipe Calderón, invited the council for lunch in the garden of Los Pinos, the presidential palace, to discuss the upcoming meeting. When the topic turned to climate, Wu Jianmin, a top Chinese diplomat and executive director of the China Institute for Innovation and Development Strategy, related that a top priority of the then incoming Party leadership of Xi Jinping would be “ecological civilization.”

All those 14 years ago, he confidently laid out a trajectory of China’s decisive shift to electric vehicles and plans for massive R&D investment in battery storage for wind and solar as well as EVs. Everyone listened respectfully, but doubtfully, because China was then not even in the auto race.

In 2012, China already dominated solar panels, but the Chevy Volt was the world’s most produced EV. No nation commanded battery production, which then was only nascently entering global competition.

Wu’s confidence in China’s capacity to deliver was well-founded. Today, nearly 70% of all new car sales in China are EVs, and half of all sales globally are Chinese-made electric vehicles. China produces around 80% of the world’s batteries and holds 70% of global battery patents. Its hosts half of the entire world’s large-scale battery storage capacity, primarily to store solar and wind power for the grid when the sun isn’t shining or the wind blowing.

As part of its whole-dragon approach, China also built out the widely distributed infrastructure of rapid charging stations across the country necessary to boost EV use. It launched a strategic push to link battery storage to the grid, requiring developers to build or commission large-scale storage capacity as a condition for approval of new wind or solar installations.

China’s export of its technology has enabled the advance of large-scale batteries for integration into power grids in many countries. Some 70% of EV batteries worldwide are from China.

California has the most installed large battery storage facilities outside of China. Its capacity has grown from a mere 700 megawatts in 2019 to 21,000 MW in 2026. By 2045, the state aims to reach 52,000 MW capacity to support a 100% clean energy grid. For the entire month of May 2026, 51% of California’s total energy demand came from solar power. Blackouts during the intense heatwaves of recent years have been avoided because the grid was linked to off-hour battery storage from renewable energy.

Though often assembled in California, 90% of the cells and core components of the large-scale batteries the state has installed come from China.

Quotas And Dumping

From the standpoint of the race against time on climate, the widest possible dispersion of China’s green technology is a net plus for the planet. Yet, as in other realms of trade competition, its cheaper product and overproduction portends a vulnerable dependence on a political system which the West considers a strategic adversary.

To the extent domestic industries exist, China’s prowess threatens to run them out of business. Since green technology is critical to our future, the most sensible approach would not be to prohibit Chinese imports, but set a reasonable quota beyond which tariffs would kick in. That would both limit the damage while allowing competition from abroad to spark the scale-up of domestic industry.

Free-market ideologues aside, subsidies are not the end of the world when a livable biosphere is at stake. After all, up until the Trump administration, the U.S. did manage for a time to escape the pull of consumer immediacy. For years, it subsidized the purchase of EVs with tax rebates. And California has shown how regulation creates, not destroys, markets. Elon Musk’s Tesla empire would never have emerged if it were not for the state’s fuel efficiency and clean energy standards, which created the market for his technology.

“Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China?”

Is It Impolitic To Learn From China?

Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China? This is not, of course, to imply in any way that the West turn toward autocracy or authoritarianism. It is only to warn that unless democracies can look beyond the short-term horizon and find ways to reach a governing consensus that sticks, they will be left in the dust of the oncoming future.

To turn an old Chinese saying toward ourselves: “The stones from hills yonder can polish jade at home.”

stories.title: Arctic Wildlife Research Suffers as Geopolitical Competition Grows
stories.summary: As national security and the hunt for rare minerals come to dominate Arctic agendas, governments are slashing support for wildlife research. Scientists say the loss of monitoring is unprecedented and comes as climate change dramatically reshapes life in the Far North. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A polar bear on sea ice in the Arctic Ocean. Sebnem Coskun / Anadolu via Getty Images

As national security and the hunt for rare minerals come to dominate Arctic agendas, governments are slashing support for wildlife research. Scientists say the loss of monitoring is unprecedented and comes as climate change dramatically reshapes life in the Far North.

By Ed Struzik • October 15, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Decades ago, one of the world’s largest subpopulations of nesting eider ducks spent its summers on tiny Mitivik Island, near the mouth of Hudson Bay. But as concern grew, in the 1990s, over their steep decline globally, the Canadian government set up a rudimentary research station near the island in the hopes of forestalling a collapse.

The modest investment paid enormous dividends over the next 30 years as Inuit partners from nearby Southampton Island, who hunt common and king eiders for food and feathers, worked with scientists from all over the world to solve the mystery of where the birds spent their winters and the causes of, and remedy for, their initial decline. In the field for months at a time, researchers also gained critical insights into how climate change, disease, diminishing sea ice, and polar bears were affecting bird populations.

As remarkably successful as the pioneering research station was, though, Canada’s Environment and Climate Change department quietly shut it down in 2024. By then, the number of nesting eiders had crashed again, from a high of 8,000 pairs to just a few hundred.

Today, federal research continues in only three of the 14 migratory bird sanctuaries in the Arctic. Hundreds of other wildlife research endeavors in the circumpolar world, including in Greenland and the U.S., have also been shuttered in recent years.

Support for Arctic research has always ebbed and flowed, says a scientist. “But what we are seeing now is unprecedented.”

Like many other agencies and programs operated by Environment and Climate Change Canada, the Canadian Wildlife Service has suffered from the high cost of conducting research in the Arctic, the increasing likelihood of polar bear encounters as sea ice recedes, and a series of crushing funding cuts. In the most recent blow, the Canadian government in 2025 committed to reducing the Environment and Climate Change workforce by 10 percent .

In the past, funding to monitor wildlife in the Arctic often had to be justified by its relevance to oil and gas development and how roads, pipelines, and oil wells would affect animals such as migrating caribou, according to Larry Hinzman, an expert in Arctic change at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. But as the search for Arctic oil and gas began to ramp down in the late 2000s, due to low natural gas prices and breakthroughs in fracking for oil and gas that spurred new production in the south, climate change became a priority.

The current circumpolar decline in funding, Hinzman said, is not just about rising costs. It stems from governments shifting priorities once again, this time from climate change to national security issues and the search for rare minerals. According to the Harvard Kennedy School’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, geopolitical tensions are also undermining the work of the Arctic Council, an international forum comprising the eight Arctic countries that plays a key role in monitoring environmental changes in the region.

Wildlife technician Uli Steiner tags a king eider netted on Mitivik Island before research efforts were halted in 2024. Grant Gilchrist

While support for research in the Arctic wanes, Canada is investing $405 million to advance the construction of a new highway to the Arctic coast to facilitate resource development and connect remote communities, part of a $40 billion plan to assert sovereignty over its Arctic territory.

Research in Alaska has been particularly hard hit by the suspension of hundreds of climate-based collaborations with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, and by the closure last year of the Arctic Research Consortium of the United States after the National Science Foundation eliminated its operating grants. Between 2021 and 2024, the number of U.S. research publications on climate change in Greenland fell by 32 percent . And in July the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the territory’s leading environmental research center, temporarily halted any new collaboration with U.S. partners when President Donald Trump threatened to take over the island.

“There have always been ebbs and flows in the support for environmental monitoring in the Arctic,” said Hinzman. “But what we are seeing now is unprecedented. It’s heartbreaking because we need to know more than ever how to respond to a warming Arctic that is affecting almost every facet of life.”

The decline in Arctic research comes at a time when at least 96 Arctic and sub-Arctic mammal and bird species may be responding to warmer winters, earlier spring snowmelt, and profound landscape changes by migrating earlier in the year and traveling farther afield, sometimes in new directions.

Studies from a now shuttered Hudson Bay research station led to tighter regulations on hunting that fueled an eider resurgence.

But dozens of studies have shown that these journeys don’t always lead to more food. And they often expose birds to additional parasites and pathogens and put them at greater risk of predation. The new migrations also happen at a time when critical stopover sites — like the Salton Sea, in California — are being badly degraded by drought and development.

Polar bears and eiders are among the many animals that appear to be struggling with rapidly warming northern marine environments, from the Baltic to the Canadian Arctic Ocean to the eastern seaboard , stretching from Newfoundland to Maine. But without researchers in the field, it’s difficult to predict how or whether these species may adapt.

The situation was far different when eiders began their mysterious worldwide decline in the 1990s. Then, researchers working in Mitivik, in the East Bay Migratory Bird Sanctuary, which would later be named the Qaqsauqtuuq Migratory Bird Sanctuary, implanted satellite transmitters into the abdomens of eiders and learned where they were overwintering. The findings led to tighter regulations on eider hunting in Canada and Greenland that dramatically boosted eider numbers.

That is, until they crashed again due to disease and polar bear predation. In 2005, Grant Gilchrist, the founder of the research station, and his colleagues identified an outbreak of avian cholera — which is rare in the Arctic and likely linked to global warming — that would kill as many as 3,000 nesting females in 2006 and about half the population over the eight seasons it spread through the nesting colony.

U.S. soldiers conduct cold-weather training near Fairbanks, Alaska, in February, after President Trump threatened to invade Greenland. Victor J. Blue / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Gilchrist was also on hand to witness how receding sea ice, brought on by climate change, forced polar bears onto land just when the eiders were sitting on their eggs. “The bears were like grazing cows leisurely moving through a pasture, stopping to feed [on eggs] whenever they were hungry,” he said. And herring gulls, which can’t force an eider off its nest, learned to eat the eggs that the bears had missed while the eiders were away.

Canadian Wildlife Service scientist Jennifer Provencher and her colleagues discovered that even though the eiders nesting in Mitivik hosted larger-than-expected communities of gastrointestinal worms and flukes, which benefit from warming temperatures, the parasites reduced the ducks’ exposure to contaminants such as mercury and lead. The parasites appear to absorb and clear contaminants from eider tissues. This is significant because mercury and lead, which are leaching from melting permafrost in many parts of the Arctic, can result in reproductive failure in ducks, and they can be harmful to humans who rely on ducks for food. The Inuit have higher levels of mercury than the general Canadian population.

Other researchers found that eiders, like some other animals exposed to deadly disease, eventually developed an immunity to avian cholera.

“Had we not been there, we would never have been able to document any of this,” said Gilchrist, who says he has little doubt that most of what Mitivik researchers discovered is happening in other parts of the Arctic.

Determining how polar bears are faring in Canada is becoming difficult, if not impossible, because of a lack of funding, a scientist says.

In the past, Indigenous hunters have reported dramatic changes in the Canadian Arctic, such as sharp declines in ivory gull numbers; orcas moving into the region and killing narwhal and bowhead whales; and grizzly bears migrating north, mating with polar bears, and producing hybrids. But it is almost impossible to say what is going on in the vast areas that are too far afield for Inuit hunters without putting scientists in the field. In Arctic Canada, there are approximately 150,000 people living in an area that is about half the size of the Lower 48 states. Only a fraction of these people lives above the Arctic Circle.

Environment and Climate Change Canada did not respond to questions about funding cuts and the cessation of research in Mitivik. In a statement, the department said it is “committed to the long-term conservation of biological biodiversity and abundance,” noting that experts are working on new research programs with territorial governments and Indigenous organizations, and with new technologies to help track and understand birds and other animals, including polar bears.

Still, Andrew Derocher, a University of Alberta scientist who has conducted research over the past 40 years on polar bears in Norway, Canada, and Alaska, notes that support for polar bear research in Canada is at an all-time low. Determining how polar bears are faring in Canada — which is home to 13 of the world’s 19 polar bear populations — is becoming increasingly difficult, he says, if not impossible, because of a lack of government funding.

Eiders found dead after an avian cholera outbreak on Mitivik Island in 2006. Grant Gilchrist

“We’ve pretty much stopped any research beyond the long-term monitoring in Western Hudson Bay and a project in James Bay” funded by a private foundation, he says. “There is almost no other research on polar bears in Canada now.”

Ornithologist Mark Mallory spent 12 years conducting research at migratory bird nesting sites across the Canadian Arctic while working for the Canadian Wildlife Service, but he left that job for a research chair at Acadia University in part because of the high cost of conducting research in the polar regions and the endless struggle to secure consistent funding. Mallory is still very much interested in what is happening in the Arctic, but his years in the field and as co-editor-in-chief of the journal Arctic Science have given him a broader perspective on the challenges scientists face when trying to figure out how a warming climate is affecting wildlife.

“No credible scientist would deny that not enough is being invested in long-term monitoring,” he says. “But the bigger problem is not enough is being done to act on what we know is happening… Do we really think 10 or 20 more years of data showing ranges shrinking north, or clutch sizes reducing, or skinnier species is going to change anything in the minds of politicians or the public?”

Gilchrist appreciates Mallory’s frustrations with governments that refuse to act on climate change, but he — like many Arctic researchers — still believes that long-term monitoring with Inuit partners is essential. “Somebody should still be out in nature monitoring wildlife and the natural environment, and quantifying changes that are occurring or not occurring,” he said.

He doesn’t know whether the eiders of Mitivik Island will eventually return or whether they have found safer areas to nest. Because of the high costs of operating at Qaqsauqtuuq and the increased odds of running into polar bears, Gilchrist is now focusing his research at a site on Baffin Island, where it is cheaper to work and where there are fewer bears.
