stories.title: What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings
stories.summary: The post What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
During the slow disintegrations of the climate crisis, choices about what to preserve become politically and culturally fraught.

Kat Hill is a writer and researcher based in Scotland. Her forthcoming book is “ Endlings: A Journey into the Last of Things .” She has held fellowships and positions at numerous academic institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study and Oxford University. She is currently the creative director of Upland Arts Development in Scotland.

Nicholas J.R. White is a photographer living on the Isle of Skye. He is a recipient of the Royal Photographic Society Environmental Bursary and is the 2026 Ampersand Foundation/Photoworks Fellow.

HAPPISBURGH, England — Off the coast of Norfolk on edge of the North Sea, the ocean can seem calm, but the waters are deceptive. Beneath the marbled brown, lie sand banks and submerged mountains waiting to ensnare unsuspecting ships. Happisburgh (pronounced Hays-burro) is a small, pretty town, its narrow roads lined by houses with walls made of flint pressed into mortar. The beach roads all have names like Stone’s Throw or Cliff Top, and the sea has always been present in people’s lives. But inching ever closer for years, now its incursions are rapid and frightening.

The light changed suddenly. Over my shoulder, the sky was dark with rain that towered in hazy columns against a thunderous glow. It rolled over the beach, over the houses, falling into the sea, billowing over the crumbling cliff edge. Lightning split the blackness, and the clouds rumbled. Gulls soared like scraps of loose paper, and sand martins wheeled in a frenzy, seeking refuge. For a moment, the world had ended. Then, it was clear again: sun shining, birds calling, people laughing.

I was looking out to submerged places, out to the infamous Doggerland. Places with names and identities that no longer exist here. Not in the way they used to. Under the water, now lost to the waves, they live on in their cartographic afterlife. Eccles-on-Sea is named after a church, but the original place of worship is long gone, and the collection of bungalows that form the village hunker behind protecting dunes and a sea wall. This is the Bush Estate, a so-called Plotland community, the name given to settlements that emerged during an early 20th century movement of working-class people buying cheap land on the seaside. Most of the houses, along with St. Mary’s church, were washed away in the 17th century; for a time, only the tower remained, the sea creeping closer and sand drifting over the stones at its base. For years, it acted as a sailor’s beacon until it too succumbed to the waves. Now, only a fragment of the bottom wall apparently remains visible at a low spring tide, though I did not see it. Dunwich, a thriving port town just to the south along the coast, was swept to sea centuries earlier.

They remain a warning to us all of what may befall a place, consigned to ruin, memory and legend.

We live at a time when endings are all around us. But endings are never straightforward. An ending may be made up of many moments. Sometimes, we don’t know when things have truly receded from our world, and it can be difficult to determine what to care about, how and when. Questions about what to save become terribly real.

Standing on the Norfolk coast, I thought how odd it was to both observe an ending and to be caught up in it. In one sense, the decline is apparent and unavoidable: Cliffs have crumbled, houses are gone, the end has happened. But in another, it’s an ending in a constant process of becoming, never starting or finishing, always ongoing. Such a loss carries emotional and philosophical weight across time, where salvation and survival ebb and flow.

The communities here seemed to be in the middle of a slow war, waiting for an enemy who would inevitably arrive no matter what watch they keep. It was an apocalyptic feeling: dark skies, rock defenses, the bones of former homes, tumbledown walls and shattered fences. And yet, the apocalypse seemed simultaneously distant, like a thing of fable, impossible to actually happen.

Writing after World War I, after the destruction wrought on the confidence of Europe, essayist Paul Valéry reflected: “W ⁠ e had long heard tell of whole worlds that had vanished, of empires sunk without a trace. … But the disasters that had sent them down were, after all, none of our affair. Elam, Nineveh, Babylon were but beautiful vague names.” Yet then, he too felt that same fear of collapse after witnessing the horror of war and the devastated world that came after. “We are aware now that a civilisation has the same fragility as a life.” Worlds can end. Choose to look, and absence and scars tell stories.

“No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender.”

“How can we learn to die?” the philosophers Fernando Flores and B. Scot Rousse asked. But confronting us today is not just individual death, nor even the prospect of human extinction, but the possibility of the disappearance of all our ways of life and being. This is what Jonathan Lear called ontological vulnerability, the sense that a world of meaning might collapse. His book “Radical Hope” was focused on the Crow people of the American West and referred to an “uncanny sense of menace … a shared vulnerability that we cannot quite name.” As Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow, said shortly before he died in 1932: “When the buffalo went away the hearts of my people fell to the ground, and they could not lift them up again. After this nothing happened.”

On the Norfolk coast, the pub, the church, the road and the shop might all soon be gone. Maybe the homes will remain, maybe not. Climate change may not kill everyone, but it may destroy the things that give life meaning. It’s one thing to survive, another to live. When you know that the flood will rush in, the fire will burn, the end is coming, what would you do? And what would you save? One option is to improve defenses: shelter cities and rebuff the rising tide from California to Yorkshire to Pacific islands. Another solution is to move.

In the U.K., the Shoreline Management Plans (SMPs), a series of complex strategic outlines, determine the futures of coastal regions, weighing up priority places to spend money and build walls. They read like military plans. The options are do nothing, maintain defenses, extend defenses or realign coastal assets. Hold the line. Fortify. Resist. Retreat.

In some instances, we have no choice but to protect something because it would do too much damage to leave it undefended. There are nuclear power plants in vulnerable places along the U.K. coast. Sizewell B in Suffolk had been slated to be decommissioned by 2035 but was recently given a new lease of life until 2055; Sizewell C, is newly under construction and due to be operational in the 2030s. It has an elaborate defense plan: raised up on a 7-meter (23-foot) platform with walls. Some say it’s not high enough. Modeling of sea level rise goes to 2140 and doesn’t take into account the long future of nuclear waste. Moreover, walls and floodgates were designed for receding high waters, not permanent rise. They endanger places nearby by preventing the natural movement of sand.

Sellafield, on the Cumbrian Coast, is the most dangerous nuclear site in Europe. It’s always present, the golf ball dome and the chimneys looming in the distance, a crumbling facade behind the farm shops and fells of the Lake District. At night the lights glow with an ominous red haze. It is a hazardous place. High-level waste is stored in legacy silos and ponds. The Magnox Swarf Silo is just leaking into the ground. ⁠ Just down the road, with armored fences on the edge of people’s homes, is the LLW Repository, the dumping ground for all low-level nuclear waste in the U.K. Long-term, the authorities aim to bury all this in the sea, deep down in a Geological Disposal Facility. But for now, they shore them up against the rising sea because to do otherwise would risk it all leaching out in catastrophic fashion. Toxic waste that never becomes safe and cannot be moved will have to be fortified.

The houses on Braystones Beach below Sellafield will not be afforded the same protection. Once, they were railway carriages that brought and housed the workers to build the line along the coast; now, some have been developed into dwellings. Like the Plotland homes of Norfolk, they are marginal communities, places pushed to the edge. Winter high tides have a 7-meter (23-foot) range, with storms whipping up surging waves, ⁠ and the row of single-story dwellings will often have the sea lapping at their doors; rocks and buoys, dredged up and dragged into shore, crash against homes. The inhabitants are determined to stay: They like living here in the wildness and wind. It’s part of the attraction, one woman told me, but they have resorted to building their own walls by claiming boulders and piling gravel and stones into embankments in front of their homes. I stood on the hill above and the small low-slung huts looked like a wall surrounding a fortress, a kind of defense protecting the aging nuclear plant. The Cumbria Coastal Strategy is dismissive of the value of the huts: “The majority of the frontage is undefended and there is no economic justification to providing significant investment at the present time.”

Famously, in 2019, the media condemned a seaside village in Wales called Fairbourne to be abandoned to the sea. House prices plummeted overnight, investment trickled away and the residents were labeled as Britain’s first climate refugees. Locals mobilized against the process of “managed retreat,” but the reputational damage was done and trust was destroyed. Insurance policies, which after all are a bet on the future, often will no longer cover homes in these coastal places.

“Choose to look and absence and scars tell stories.”

There are already ruins and remnants aplenty on the Norfolk coast. It’s littered with the remains of Norman castles and military lookouts. Of all the things we could protect, is it worth saving ruins? Should we simply let them be committed to the memory of the sea? They are more than crumbling walls or upturned pillboxes — they are reminders of our past, anchors that root us to a sense of history and landscape. Just like with everything else, there’ll only be certain ruins designated as important and worth protecting. This is true of any heritage site, not just those threatened by climate change. As Gavin Lucas writes, “entropy is a social as well as a natural phenomenon.”

A recent National Trust report admitted it could not contain threats to coastal sites and aims to work “with the grain of nature.” On the coast of Caithness in Scotland’s far northeast, there are castles at every bay and promontory exposed to the ravages of the sea. One, Castle Sinclair Girnigoe, an impressive northern fortress, was listed on the World Monument Fund’s Monuments Watch in 2002. The complex of structures, dating back to the 15th century and once owned by Clan Sinclair, has received funds to stabilize and conserve the structure. Just along the coast, however, is Castle Bucholie, listed by Historic Environment Scotland, but without the same resources to protect it from its fate. Read Noema in print.

“Old” ruins were once homes or lives. The world is ephemeral. Preservation suggests we can protect things in the future by putting them on lists, but that’s not really true. The Caithness castles lean into the sea, and the empty windows look out to the water like screaming faces. Girnigoe Sinclair reopened with much fanfare in 2010, but the slow creep of time continues regardless of how much attention is given to it. Transience may be an opportunity to tell complex stories though; “managed ruination” can be a way to write what the cultural geographer Caitlin DeSilvey refers to as an “anticipatory history” of absence.

When I visited, Castle Sinclair’s wooden drawbridge was closed and the walls were covered in scaffolding. It is being reclaimed not just by the sea but by nature. Nesting fulmars stared from a window, and marsh orchids were growing out of the turf that covered the ruined walls.

Sea level rise and climate change threaten the nonhuman world, too. I saw ringed plovers on the beach near Sellafield, sand martins on the crumbling cliffs of the Norfolk coast. Signs warn people away from their nesting sites.

Norfolk’s water systems — the great expanses of the Broads, mudflats and marshes — are increasingly susceptible to the incursion of salty waves. The complex estuarine networks are like arteries that get pumped full of seawater when storm surges come. Salty waters kill invertebrates on which nesting waders feed, and wash away habitat.

Nonhuman environments are being squeezed, but who wants to save the sand martins or the butterflies when homes and businesses are at risk? Something must be sacrificed, and “sacrifice zone” is a term becoming increasingly common in discussions about environmental justice. It’s a word in the language of sanctity, martyrdom and faith — an act of giving something up to a higher purpose, to a god or to a devil. It asks that we think about death as something. It asks that we consider who to make a victim. If we build sea walls, we destroy marshland. If we protect nuclear waste, we condemn coastal communities.

No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender. As I talked to people in Norfolk, Cumbria and Scotland, the rising sea was ever present in their minds, yet they were also persistent and stubborn. This was their home. What else were they supposed to do?

Endings are not neat, and it’s unclear when an ending is inevitable, when it is declared and who gets to declare it. Sometimes a world comes and goes in an instant but, more often, there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting. Despite it all, it’s not easy to leave the thing that gives your world meaning and stability.

On a beach railing I found on the coast of Norfolk, there’s a sticker of a man. Rocks and flowers are arranged around the picture, with words of affectionate remembrance. Nearby is a bench with an inscription to a young biker who loved the view of the sea. The bench and the flowers will be gone soon, such small but momentous reminders of the persistence of love and memory in absence. Is this the time, when past and memory are done, when “nothing happens”?

“Sometimes the world may come and go in an instant but more often there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting.”

Because that’s the thing about these decisions. They are not just cold calculations, but about love, even when an end comes. The residents in Happisburgh and nearby Mundesley are worried about the churches that are threatened by the sea, which will undermine the graves of their family members and community. At St. Mary’s in Happisburgh, there’s a mass grave for sailors who drowned in the deep. Their bones are now being returned to the sea, and with them the memory of their lives.

I wandered into the church and saw a woman tending to the flowers on the altar, a wheelbarrow full of blooms next to her. In a pew, a man sat watching her as the sun streamed in through the glass, illuminating the dancing dust. Richard and Joan have lived and worked here all their lives, both baptized in the centuries-old font.

“One day the sea will take it.” That’s what she says. She knows this is true but she tends the church anyway because it is part of her past. It dates to the 14th century; its peal of eight bells ring every Wednesday. There are legends around here that you can hear the drowned bells of Dunwich or Eccles-on-Sea. I’ve heard a similar tale of the mythical city of Ys, submerged beneath the waves, whose cathedral bell still rings.

There’s another bell on the beach at Happisburgh, designed by artist Marcus Vergette, that rings with the tide. Vergette told me that the bell was the perfect design for the sea. Bells disrupt space. They have a history and personality; they have names. Bells rang for death and life, funeral and marriage, celebration, announcement, mourning or warning. They communicate the passing of time and the ritual of life, and a bell’s back and forthness expresses the liminality of the coast. It is, he said, a particularly suitable form for the shifting sands of life, and to express the ambiguity of loss and desire.

I stood on the beach and listened to it. It tolled for time, for tide, for life and death. It was a liturgy of loss, but it was also a celebration and a call to joy and worship, perhaps even hope or the new dawn of a day.

What hope could it ring for? Lear believed in the vulnerability of our world but also a kind of radical hope even in absence and loss. Perhaps those places that are gone could have an afterlife. Recently archaeologists recorded oral histories around Happisburgh and scanned and 3D-photographed the church so it can live on in some form. Whole countries are adopting this approach. Tuvalu, a Pacific Island nation comprising small islets and low-lying atolls, is aiming to become the first “digital nation.” Seen from the air it is a ring of land in a backdrop of blue, a thin coral halo sinking rapidly. Tuvalu will not accept its fate as a victim; it will not just give into the inevitable end handed to it by the global forces of destruction.

Radical hope is possible, Lear writes, because we can have courage. Courage is an important virtue because it recognizes that we are “finite erotic creatures. … As finite creatures we are vulnerable: we may suffer physical and emotional injury, we may make significant mistakes, even the concepts with which we understand ourselves and the world may collapse — and yet as erotic creatures we reach out to the world and try to embrace it.”

I caught the last light of the day at the church in Mundesley. The golden sun escaped from underneath the granite clouds and it washed the world gold. Just for a moment. A great rainbow arced overhead, a sign of hope and peace after the storm, the color that returned after the biblical flood.

There may not be a world of pure hope for these coastal villages, because there will be losses. Even with an ending, we can consider what practices of courage, care and value to adopt, and what can be salvaged as we build defenses, remember and protect elsewhere. The economy of salvation is never straightforward, so reach out and embrace the world even as it disappears.

stories.title: Scientists Are Teaching Birds to Sing Lost Songs
stories.summary: When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A rufous-collared sparrow. Charles J. Sharp via Wikipedia

When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs.

Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area.

That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.

There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect,” they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory, and ultimately survive.

If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers. Birds can begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species , jeopardizing their chances of breeding.

Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well — which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently, and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy, you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo.

“When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B. Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who coauthored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds .

But animals’ learned behavior or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin.

The rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist.

About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows, and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds, has identified common “motifs” or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes, and harmonic notes.

The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range.

The song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out.

It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined.

Birds’ songs can change naturally over time — for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes.

Songbirds learn from other members of their species — such as a father or neighbors — which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge.

“There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behavior at the University of Plymouth, who studied a group of cirl buntings that were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project.

Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal.

A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says.

Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated.

A separate study in Australia tracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation.

“Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins.

Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that A.I. could help provide live tutoring in the future.

Dialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarizing birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this.

A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.”

In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists.

— Rebecca Ratcliffe , The Guardian

stories.title: PM says youth unemployment is a 'catastrophe and a moral failure'
stories.summary: The UK faces "economic catastrophe" with one million young people not in work or training, the prime minister says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Britain needs to "invest in the success of our young people", Andy Burnham says

Published 19 October 2026, 02:40 BST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Writing in the Times newspaper , external , Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.

This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.

Around 39% are unemployed while the remaining 61% are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.

The number of 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits stands at 331,000, almost double the number in 2016, but lower than the peaks of around 500,000 seen after the financial crisis in 2008 and Covid in 2020.

The UK government will spend £353bn on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is spent on benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments.

In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.

Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.

"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."

He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".

"We either invest in the success of our young people or pay for failure through the benefits system. We cannot afford to do both," Burnham wrote.

Ministers are this week set to release plans for 22,400 apprenticeships a year in businesses such as accountants, legal services and consultants, in addition to 40,000 placements in the construction industry.

The Conservative shadow business and trade secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."

The party has said they would cut £36bn a year from the welfare budget including by reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit and restricting who receives housing benefit.

Green Party deputy co-leader Mothin Ali accused Labour of planning a "welfare cuts charter that would take support away from young people who are already struggling and vulnerable".

What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many? Published 27 August

Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor Published 28 September

Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".

While the prime minister has emphasised the importance of incentivising young people into work, the review's author Alan Milburn suggested there could be cuts to benefits.

The former health secretary told the Guardian , external that there was a need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support".

"This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."

Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful" .

In order to cut the benefit bill, both Burnham and Milburn will need to secure the support of those Labour MPs who previously baulked at Sir Keir Starmer's attempts to reduce spending by £5bn a year.

Backbenchers objected to proposals to tighten restrictions for those claiming working-age health-related benefits and, following a rebellion, the then-prime minister was forced to abandon his plans.

Two of Burnham's closest supporters Louise Haigh, his effective deputy, and Anneliese Midgley, his chief whip, who are now in government, were both leading lights in the welfare rebellion.

But difficult decisions are coming nonetheless and government insiders are clear that the link between cuts to welfare entitlement to fund increased jobs support is inevitable.

While Burnham has promised not to introduce "crude cuts", Labour advisers say it is impossible to leave the system for under 25s unchanged.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden is sympathetic to Milburn's call for a new, parallel benefits system for young people - but that level of change will require legislation.

Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, and there is not expected to be much mention of welfare in it.

Instead a bill is being prepared and the New Year is when that is likely to be voted on by MPs.

stories.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
stories.summary: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026, 01:22 BST

Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise".

The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

The rail campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000.

The government also said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff "or the British Transport Police if they wish".

"They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said.

Justin from Newcastle-upon-Tyne, welcomed the proposal but wanted to know how it would be enforced.

He told the BBC noise on public transport had stopped him from using buses "due to the levels of antisocial behaviour including this unwanted attendance to someone's social media doom scrolling audio concert".

He said he'd "much rather enjoy my own company with my own music in the isolation of my car".

Transport for London, which operates London Underground, already has byelaws in place to prohibit people playing music or content aloud.

It said that in the first instance enforcement officers will ask the passenger to stop.

"Most people comply at this stage," it said, but added that if someone refuses, they may be asked to leave the train or they could be reported for possible prosecution.

The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".

However, she added the government must "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers".

"Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.

Dave McAra from Derby got in touch with the BBC to raise a similar point: "Who is going to police this legislation on a bus? The solo driver? I think not as he would probably be verbally abused at best and assaulted at worst."

Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise Published 6 August

Reported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a third Published 24 September

Safety concerns put Londoners off buses, say Tories Published 11 July

Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs.

He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."

Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the Conservative Party had "led the charge" against antisocial behaviour on public transport last year.

However, he added passengers and railway staff faced more serious problems.

"Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways," he said.

Liberal Democrat transport spokesperson Olly Glover said: "Unless the government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."

Independent watchdog Transport Focus said its research showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway.

"Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell from Transport Focus.

"Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

stories.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
stories.summary: The chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee says families should not be taxed through no fault of their own.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026, 12:34 BST

Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.

Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.

The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.

However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Published 12 February

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Published 29 January

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo Published 23 January

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.

The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.

If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.

Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".

His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.

Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".

He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".

He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."

Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong?

Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions

Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.

On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.

Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.

"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."

Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.

However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.

Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

Rob is hoping the government will waive the tax due for people in his situation

Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.

"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.

"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.

"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."

A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.

"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops looted

Business live – latest updates

France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.

The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.

The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.

This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.

Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.

“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.

“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”

The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.

Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.

Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.

Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.

Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.

“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.

The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.

The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit .

France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.

after newsletter promotion

The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.

“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”

The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.

The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.

France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.

French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.

Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.

“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

Watch: Polanski says practical application of Zionism is racist

Published 18 October 2026

Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership .

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.

"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.

"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

'All over the place'

Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said he did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."

Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland.

"I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said.

"I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."

When questioned if he thought Israel had a right to exist, he said he did not think "any state has a right to exist under international law".

And asked if he would apologise for his handling of the row, as the Jewish Greens chair Vivien Lichtenstein has asked him to do, Polanski said: "I'm not sorry at all."

In response, Phil Rosenberg, president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, accused Polanski of being "all over the place" on the issue.

"Let us remember that, as of now, the Green Party's platform erases Jewish identity and experience, calls for Israel's elimination, and tells the vast majority of Jews, who overwhelmingly believe in the right of Israel to exist, that they are not welcome in the party," Rosenberg added.

Polanski has said no Jewish Green members will be excluded based on their faith or background - and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are "two separate things".

His latest comments come after a fortnight of criticism from across the political spectrum over the motion.

Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "antisemitic". Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

No patient should be treated in a corridor, Yvette Cooper says

Published 18 October 2026

The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

The health secretary has announced £140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

Two-year-old Finlay Roberts died after spending hours in a crowded hospital corridor

The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened extended their condolences to the family.

They said they continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.

"Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions," they said.

On Friday health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), also expressed their concern over corridor care, writing a letter to the health secretary urging her to take action.

It said the practice was fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.

This weekend Cooper announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.

The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.

Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from.

It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.

Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.

NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying earlier this month there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.

Swords said there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year.

RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point".

"The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.

stories.summary: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge. stories.body:
In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China

There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.

Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.

In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.

The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.

Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level.

It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.

Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square .

A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule.

Then came AI and the state discovered complete control.

Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to.

Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished.

For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world.

Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology.

Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions.

Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights.

Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents.

There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers.

after newsletter promotion

In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need.

Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented . But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option.

As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation.

He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.”

An evaluation report by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship.

“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says.

The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities.

Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assume data inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state .

The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers.

Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.

Published 19 October 2026, 16:25 BST

Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France .

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

Reports suggest eBay has seen similar activity on its platform. The BBC has contacted the website for comment.

French PM calls for partial curfews as he condemns 'thieves' and 'thugs' behind riots

Reuters news agency reported luxury shops and boutiques were shuttered and surrounded by security guards at the Place Vendome in Paris.

But it said a host of stores in the French capital, including Dior, Rolex, Louis Vuitton and Ralph Lauren had their shopfronts damaged

In Marseille, football club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted.

It has closed the store, along with fellow Ligue 1 club Lille, which said its club shop would remain closed until further notice.

stories.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
stories.summary: Gritty HBO series is a beacon for what's possible when one is allowed to get creative with the tropes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Gritty HBO series is a beacon for what’s possible when one is allowed to get creative with the tropes.

The trailers for HBO’s DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detectives or Slow Horses . Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing ; it’s wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegaic finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre.

(Spoilers below, but no major reveals.)

There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn’t think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal’s power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains.

Hal and John soon discover that the suspect was one of a group of aliens who survived a genocide on their home planet committed by so-called Manhunters : a race of extraterrestrial beings created by the Guardians of the Universe as a forerunner to the Lantern Corps. The Manhunters rebelled against the Guardians, and most were killed; the sole survivor is hiding out in Rushville disguised as a human. The alien leader, Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor), gives Hal and John 48 hours to locate the Manhunter and hand them over, or they will destroy the town.

The second storyline takes place in 2026 and concerns the murder of none other than Hal Jordan, who returned to Rushville as a social pariah after the terrible events that transpired 10 years before. That mystery becomes the focus of the second half of the series, as Stewart teams up with the sheriff to solve Hal’s murder.

Green Lantern’s light

The entire cast brings their A game to their portrayals, and you couldn’t ask for better leads than Chandler and Pierre, both of whom have plenty of meaty, substantial material to work with. Showrunner Chris Mundy has said that one of the major themes of the show is deciding when it’s time for one person to step aside and let a replacement take over, embodied in the push and pull of Hal and John’s relationship. The two men are very different personalities: Hal is cocky, arrogant, and trusts his gut instincts; John is controlled, disciplined, logical, and methodical. Hal has no intention of giving up the power ring; John questions whether Hal really deserves it. Naturally they’re going to clash, and given the stakes, that conflict has severe consequences, both for them and the town.

But there is so much more to these characters than their surface personalities. Both have daddy issues, for instance: Hal because he lost his father at a young age, John because his father was passed over to be a Green Lantern and made John’s entire childhood about making up for his failure. John has been groomed by his parents—under the watchful eye of the Guardians—to eventually replace the rule-defying and frequently reckless Hal, who lost both parents. It’s to the writers’ credit that exploring these issues doesn’t come off like a cliché therapy session, instead adding depth and emotional resonance.

Lanterns works so well in part because it was conceived as a standalone complete story, albeit one with ramifications for future DCU projects, thereby freeing up the writers to create something truly unique, with no forced, awkward tie-ins. Even Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner, aka Green Lantern 2026, fits seamlessly into the plot. Nor do you need to be a fan of the Green Lantern comics and associated lore to follow along, although there are plenty of Easter eggs embedded throughout.

That said, this is a densely plotted series with lots of characters. Fortunately, the show maintains a leisurely but never sluggish pace to ensure one can follow all the twists and turns, and savor the richly layered characters with their complex interrelationships, quite well. And the two parallel mysteries will keep you guessing right to the very end. Between Peacemaker and Lanterns , HBO has done right by the DCU, with the Jimmy Olsen (Skylar Gisondo) series The People v. Gorilla Grodd —described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series”—coming next year. Maybe we should just let HBO take it from here.

All episodes of Lanterns are now streaming on HBO Max.

stories.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
stories.summary: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026, 00:00 BST

Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results.

He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price.

"Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price. Properties were on the market high and low but were not selling," he said.

He turned down an offer made on his home a day after it was listed. It was below the asking price and he held out for better offers that never came. In the end, he sold after 18 months for £30,000 less than the original asking price.

Colleen Babcock, of Rightmove, said: "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home.

Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price.

The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023.

Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed.

With mortgage rates at a three-year high , Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable.

So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed.

September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year.

Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price.

The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell.

Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Zoopla.

'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak? Published 19 September

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Published 28 September

Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England.

One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."

Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".

But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.

Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial.

"That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.

Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price.

"The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.

But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.

In Scotland, the Home Report system , external requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market.

Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain.

His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London.

He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England.
